EWE: Ne nyɔnu aɖe le evi dzim eye wo le kukum nɛ la, o wɔna kɔnu na ɖevi yeye si wo ga dzi la, to ŋkɔ bubu tsɔtsɔ nɛ la me, bena ɖevi yeyela me ga ku ke o.
ENGLISH: ﻿If a woman often loss his baby after he is born, people make a kind of ceremony for the new one born, and this ceremony is about giving to the new baby another name that help the newest stay alive.

EWE: Ŋkɔ sia nye na ŋkɔ si ke ame bubu tsɔna na ɖevia si gɔme enye be ehɔ ɖevi la ƒle le ƒomea si.
ENGLISH: This name comes from another person, which means that this person buys the baby from the biologic parents.

EWE: Ame si hɔ ɖevi la ƒlela tsona ƒome bubu me alo dukɔ bubume alo edu bubume alo amedzro tso duta, vɔa nyui tɔ enye be amea ne nye amedzro tso duta.
ENGLISH: This person must not be part of the whole family of the baby, he must be from another family, another village, another city or another region or ethnical group or another country, but the best situation is when this person is from another country (foreigner).

EWE: Kɔnua wo yina ale: evinɔ si ga dzi ɖevi bubu alo evi yeye la ƒe ƒomea yina ɖe mɔdododzi, he da ɖevi yeye la ɖe mɔ dodome, he yina bena ɖe gbetime alo aveme he nɔ ŋku sam na amesi ato afima afɔ ɖevi la.
ENGLISH: The ceremony is done as follow: the family of the newest baby goes on the road, and leave the baby in the middle of the road (of course not the road where cars can kill the child) and goes to hide in the bush or in the forest close to the road to see who will pass through the road and take the baby.

EWE: Ne ame aɖe vayina to afimagodzi he kɔ ɖevia la, le emayi me la ƒomea doa dzesi amema alo bena kplɔna neneŋ ƒe amea ɖo, ne wome dzesi o, he nyana afisi nye amedrola ƒe afeme alo afisi wo da ɖevilaɖoe.
ENGLISH: When somebody passes through the road and finds and takes the baby, in this time, the family notices the person and if the family doesn’t know who is it, he simply follow the person in secret to know where the person live or where the person leave the child.

EWE: Emegbe la ɖevila ƒe pomea ɖona to, he tɔna tekpɔ ekpɔ dodo tso ɖevi fɔfɔ ŋti, eye ne wose kpododo tso ɖevi fɔfɔ ŋti la, enumake wo yina he gblɔna be miavie.
ENGLISH: After then, the family simply waiting for information about a baby find on the road, and the family goes and said it is our child.

EWE: Esiao kãtã vayina le ga ƒoƒo aɖeo me.
ENGLISH: All this happen in some hours.

EWE: Ɖevi yeye la ƒe ƒomea nana mɔnu kpɔkpɔ amesi fɔ ɖevi la be woa ɖu tɔ nɛ.
ENGLISH: The family gives an opportunity to the person who finds the child to be he’s second father.

EWE: Le ɣemayi mela ame si fɔ ɖevila, nana ŋkɔ bubu si dzroe ɖevila, ŋkɔ sia ateŋ anyi Fɔfɔe alo Ofɔe alo Oƒle…… ne amesi fɔ ɖevi yeyela me na ŋkɔa ɖekee o.
ENGLISH: At this time this person gives a name he wants to the child, but this child can be named Fɔfɔe or Ofɔe or Oƒle if this person doesn’t give any name to the child.

EWE: Evi fɔla si trozu ɖevila ƒe tɔ evelia la, ateŋ ne elɔla, ahɔ ɖevila ɖe eɖokui gbɔɛ le ɖevila ƒe sisime alo ɖevima ateŋ anɔ egbɔ yim le aza dzilo alo lekuhɛ me.
ENGLISH: This person who becomes the second father of the child has close right like the biologic parents, for instance can request to raise the child of course after some years or the child can visit him in holidays or ask for help or advice in difficult situations.

EWE: Esiao wɔwɔ, hena emɔ na, eku be mega dzesi ɖevi yeye la o, elabena etɔ ŋkɔ bubu.
ENGLISH: This fact protect the child from the quickly death as this woman observes in the past for her babies because this baby has another name and the death can’t recognize him.

EWE: Edzi edzi la kadodo nɔna ɖevila ƒe ƒomea kple ɖevila ƒe tɔ evelia dome kuɖe ɖevila ƒe nyawo ŋti.
ENGLISH: Time to time the biologic family and the second father discuss about some matters connected to the child.

EWE: Ele be ma ɖo ŋku edzi be amesi fɔ ɖevila ɖo la nye ŋsu, ne me nye nenema ola, ele be woa ga gbugbɔ dze kɔnua gɔme.
ENGLISH: I have to mention that the person who finds the child must be a man another way, the ceremony must be done again in other that the person who will take the baby must be a man.

EWE: (Kɔnu sia nye kɔnuaɖe si sɔkple, ne woa gblɛ kpuiɖe ko la, Moiz ƒe ŋti nyao le bibla me).
ENGLISH: (This ceremony is close to the history about Moses in the Bible)

EWE: ETSƆ WƆWƆ LE EƲE DUKƆWOME
ENGLISH: FUNERAL CEREMONIES IN EWE ETHNICAL GROUPS LAND

EWE: Le eʋe dukɔ wome la, etsɔ ƒe kɔnu wɔwɔwo tona vovo vɔa vovo totoa me nye enu gã aɖekeo.
ENGLISH: In Ewe ethnical groups, the ceremony about funerals is different, but those differences are not so important.

EWE: Mia gblɛ kpo me, le afisiafi klui la, etsɔ ƒe wɔwɔ nye na ŋkunekame, vɔa akɔta aɖeo tsɔna kɔnu aɖewo kpenɛ.
ENGLISH: We can notice some deep ceremony in some Ewe groups, but it is just some specific add from the particular group or family.

EWE: Ne nye be ameaɖe ku le ƒome aɖe me la, wo tsɔna ame kuku la yina danaɖe frigo le dɔyɔƒe si sɔ eku ƒomea be teƒe.
ENGLISH: When one-person die in one Ewe family, the dead family brings the dead body to the closest hospital where the family will pay for place to freeze the dead body.

EWE: Ŋtilã kukula ateŋ anɔ frigo eyiyi didi aɖe alesi eku ƒomea kpɔbe yewo hiã na dzadzraɖo ne etsɔ wɔwɔ.
ENGLISH: This body can stay in freezer until the dead family realize that their ready to start the funerals.

EWE: Emegbe la, eku ƒomea yina ɖe edumegã gbɔ he sianɛ be amekuna yewo eye wo ɖena mɔ na eku ƒomea be woateŋ aɖi ameyinugbe la le edzua ƒe ameɖibɔme me.
ENGLISH: Then, the family will contact with the chief of the village or of the neighbourhood if it is in the city to have an approval to bury the dead body in the village or neighbourhood cemetery.

EWE: Le Kpalime nutowo mela, wo wɔna edumegã siasia sia tɔxɛ, wo ɖo ŋkɔ ne kɔnu sia be « eku tsitsi ».
ENGLISH: In Kpalimé region (one specific Ewe group), this approval from the chief is an important issue, they call it "eku tsitsi " that means information about the dead person.

EWE: Eku tsitsi nye ŋdi kɔnua ɖe sime dukɔa kãtã ƒonaƒu le ekpododo megbe he sena eyiyi mablɛ ƒe nya tso eku ƒomea gbɔ kuɖe ameyinugbea ŋti.
ENGLISH: This ceremony is a meeting with the chief and other people living in this neighbourhood or village in which the dead family has to tell the last moment of life of the dead person.

EWE: O wɔna eku tsitsi ƒe kɔnu edzi edzi le yawoɖa ƒe ŋkeke si kplɔna fiɖa fe ŋkeke si nyena ŋdɔdɔ ƒe ŋkeke la.
ENGLISH: This meeting hang on Thursdays that follow the Friday on which will stand the vigil.

EWE: Eku tsitsi va yina alɛ ; eku ƒomea ƒoanu kuna ɖe enusi wo dedzesi be yaye wu ame la, esia ateŋ anye edɔleleaɖe, alo edzobibi alo afɔku le mɔdododzi alo le agbleme alo le edɔme.
ENGLISH: All the meeting start as follow; the dead family speaks about the fact that is responsible for the person death, this can be sickness or disease, or fire burn, or accident on road or in farm or in office.

EWE: Ƒomea gblɔna enusi wo vayi edzi le gaƒoƒo mamlɛa ome, eye wo ƒoanu kuɖe ameyinugbea ƒe fukpekpe, kpekpeneŋ alo agbagba dzedze si wo teŋ wɔ hena ameyinugbea ƒe haya haya alo eƒe ta ʋliʋli hafi meteŋ va eme o.
ENGLISH: The family suppose to tell exactly the things that happen at the last moment, like the suffering, the help that the family provide to save his life from death before he died.

EWE: To siawɔwɔ me la, amesiwo ƒoƒu kple dumegã kple eƒe ŋtimewo bia na nya akpɔbe vodada me tso eku ƒomea gbɔ loo alo ameaɖe si le fui la gbɔ o mahã.
ENGLISH: From this information, people who stand there with the chief and his speakers will try to ask many questions to check if the family has some responsibility in this death or if this death is connected with another person that willing to short this person life.

EWE: Ne esia va va eme nenema be ekua ƒe nya kã ameaɖe alo eku ƒe ƒomea la, wo blana nu nɛ.
ENGLISH: And if is happen that anybody or the death family has some responsibility in this person death, the responsible person must pay a fee.

EWE: Neneŋ be ame ana alɛ alo egbɔ alo aha alo nububu wo hã.
ENGLISH: This fee can be goats, sheep and or some specific drinks or other things else.

EWE: Esiawo wɔwɔ tutuna kadodo vɔɖi si le ameyinugbea kple amegbagbea dome.
ENGLISH: This kind of action will delete or free the relation between the dead person and the life person.

EWE: Le esiawo megbe la, le fiɖa ŋkeke sidzi woa dɔŋu le la, wo hɔna ameyinugbea ƒe ŋtilã kuku le frigo le dɔyɔƒe eye le ŋkekea ƒe fiɛyi me alo zãgã dome la, wo va ɖona kple amekukua ƒe ŋtilã le ekutefea.
ENGLISH: After this meeting which held on Thursday, Friday night will be the vigil (spending all Friday night for the dead person), the dead family will go to the hospital and receive the dead body and in the evening or in the night, the family will arrive with the dead body in the place where they prepare everything for the last exposition of the dead body.

EWE: Vɔ hafi eyiyi mawo na vaɖo la, dukɔa mevio kpenaɖe eku ƒomea ŋti he tuna agbadɔ he na etsɔa ƒe kɔnuwo wɔwɔ.
ENGLISH: But before that time, the people from the neighborhood or from the village help the dead family to build some tent or hut for the funerals.

EWE: Ŋdɔdɔ dzena egɔme le fiɛyi me eye wo yina edzi vaseɖe ŋdikãnyɛ me.
ENGLISH: The vigil starts from the evening and continues till the next day morning.

EWE: Le ga ƒoƒo mawo mela, kɔnuawo va yina ale: gbã la, hɔse tɔwo dzena ŋdɔdɔ gɔme nenyebe ameyinugbea nye kristotɔ, eye wo wɔna misa va senaɖe zã ga wueve godzi eye wo kpana, emegbe la eʋu ƒoƒo geɖe wo va yina edzi, etsona eʋu haƒoƒo si me ameyinugbea nɔ alo eʋu haƒoƒo si eku ƒomea da be woa dodzidzɔ mablɛwo ɖe amekukua ŋuti.
ENGLISH: During this time everything go as follow: firstly, Christian starts the vigil if the dead person is believe in God, and then they observe Mass till midnight, and then the drams music will continue the vigil. This dram groups can be one of the dead person group (means that he belong to this group) or the dead family simply order music to enjoy the last moment of the death.

EWE: Vɔ gake, ne ameyinugbea me nye hɔsetɔ wola, ŋdɔdɔa va yina edzi kpakple voduʋu ƒoƒo ɖeɖeko le zã katã me.
ENGLISH: Secondly, if the dead person is belonging to any kind of fetish group, then the whole night will be covered by dram music from the fetish group.

EWE: Elebe mia do dzesi be eʋu ƒoƒo sia wo nyena enu tɔxɛ aɖe le Eʋe dukɔ ɖesiaɖe me klui.
ENGLISH: We have to notice that, this kind of specific dram music is very important and common in all Ewe regions.

EWE: Wo dzi na exa geɖe wo siwo nyena enya mamlɛwo hena emɔzɔzɔ nyui dodo na ameyinugbea.
ENGLISH: That music from dram tells in a precise and direct way good-bye and good journey to the dead person.

EWE: Le zã kãtã me la, wo ɖena emɔ ne amewo kãtã be woateŋ akpɔ ŋtilã kukula zi mablɛtɔe, he ne woateŋ ado mɔzɔzɔ nyui ne, amesiawo ateŋ anye ameyinugbea ƒe ƒomewo alo eƒe hɔlɔwo alo amesiwo kãtã dzibe yewoa do neneŋ ƒe egbe mablɛa ne.
ENGLISH: During the vigil in the memory of the dead person, it is allow for everybody to visit the dead body at his exposition. And those people can be the dead family, the friend, the relations and so on, just an opportunity for them to say personal last good-bye.

EWE: Hafi woa ɖemɔ ne amewo be woateŋ akpɔ ŋtila kukula la, wo wɔna kɔnua ɖe si wo yɔna be « abaɖoɖo » si me wo dzrana ŋtila kukuaɖo ɖe abadzi.
ENGLISH: But before this permission for visiting the dead body, they have special ceremony called "abaɖoɖo " which simply means to "prepare the bed " in which they make sleep the death in some specific way that some time you fill like the person is alive.

EWE: Vɔ gake, nenye be amekukua nye vodu hamenɔla la, ŋdɔdɔ kple ameɖiɖi ƒe kɔnuawo vayina ɖe vodua ƒe sewo dzi, gaɖeo mela, eku ƒomea me nɔna vodua ƒe kɔnua ɖewo teƒe oo.
ENGLISH: We must know that, if the dead person is disciple of fetish, the vigil and the burial ceremonies are done following the rule of the fetish, some time the dead family is not allow to follow some ceremonies done by the fetish group.

EWE: Elebe mia ɖo ŋku edzi hã be, ne nye be ameyinugbea nye vodusi la, vodu haƒoƒoa me ɖena mɔ be woa dee frigo oo.
ENGLISH: We have to remember also that, if the dead person is a member of fetish group, this group doesn’t allow the dead family to freeze the dead body.

EWE: O wɔna neneŋu be ameyinugbea ƒe etsɔ kɔnuawo kaba kaba le ŋkeke etɔ megbe le vodua ƒe ɖoɖowo nu.
ENGLISH: They simply short the term of the funerals during three days and of course according to the fetish rules.

EWE: Le ŋkeke evelia si nye memlina ƒe ŋkeke si nyena ŋkeke evelia le etsɔa ƒe kɔnuwo wɔwɔnu la, wo wɔna ame ɖiɖi ƒe kɔnuwo.
ENGLISH: The second day of the funerals is Saturday, is the burial ceremonies day.

EWE: Le ŋdi kpadzi, wo wɔna gbɔ lɔlɔ si me wo dzina nublanui hawo le, eye hafi woawɔ misa la, wo wɔna kɔnuaɖe si wo yɔna be « ame dede aɖakame ».
ENGLISH: In Saturday morning, generally women walk on the road close to the place of funerals singing pity songs to call the dead person spirit out of the Village or the neighborhood, and before the last Mass of the presence of dead body, they have another ceremony named « ame dede aɖakame » which means "put in the coffin ".

EWE: Kɔnua vayina ale: eku ƒomea kple Mawununɔla nenye be ameyinugbea nye Kristotɔ, alo eku ƒomea kple vodununɔla nenyebe ameyinugbea nye vodusi, yina ŋtilã kukula gbɔ le hɔme he denɛ aɖakame kple enya ƒoɖo aɖeo.
ENGLISH: It happen as follow, the dead family and Priest if the dead person believes in God and the representative of fetish if the dead person belong to fetish group, go to the dead body and put the body in the coffin with some specific traditional words from the dead family and the representative of the fetish group (It depend and it done according to the kind of the death).

EWE: Emegbe la wo wɔna misa alo vodu kɔnuwo he nana yayra mamlɛa ameyinugbea.
ENGLISH: After then they will observe with the people Mass or fetish ceremonies for the last benediction of the dead person.

EWE: Le emawo yome la, wo dzena mɔ yina ɖe ameɖibɔme afisi wo wɔna konu mamlɛtɔwo le he tsɔna aɖakala dena do me le.
ENGLISH: At the last moment, they will bring the coffin with the dead person to the cemetery where they pray and make the burial ceremonies.

EWE: Ne wo gbɔ tso ameɖiƒe vɔla, wo wɔna akpedada wɔna vovovowo, eye emegbe la amedzrowo xɔxɔ ƒe wɔnawo va yi na edzi kple eʋu ƒoƒo wɔna geɖewo.
ENGLISH: The third day which is Sunday, they have generally Mass for the dead person, and in evening, the dead family distribute drinks for everybody that help during the funerals; chief and people that act during ceremonies.

EWE: Le kɔsiɖa si nye ŋkeke etɔlia le etsɔ wɔwɔ ƒe wɔnawo me la, wo wɔna misa ɖe ameyinugbea ta, eye le fiɛyi mela, wo wɔa aha mama ƒe kɔnuwo he dana akpe na amesiame si kpede eku ƒomea ŋti le wɔna vovovoa wome.
ENGLISH: We have to mention that funerals ceremonies make a lot of spending on the expense of the dead family, and often the dead family borrow money to cover the spending to show how wealthy is the family.

EWE: Elebe miaɖo ŋku edzi hã be, etsɔ kɔnu siawo wɔwɔ nyena ega zãzã geɖe ɖe nɔna eku ƒomea dzi, eye edzi edzi la ameyinugbe ƒomewo dona ga asɔ wɔ tsoɛ bene woateŋ ahɔ kɔkɔ le wo havio gbɔ.
ENGLISH: It is a king of competition between families to show their capacity (It doesn’t make sense, but is how it works in Ewe ethnical groups).

EWE: Etsɔ wɔwɔ nye enu hɔasiaɖe le Eʋe dukɔwo ƒe kɔta kɔnu wɔwɔwome.
ENGLISH: The funeral ceremonies are very important ones among Ewe community’s ceremonies.

EWE: Enyena eyiyi sime eku ƒomea ƒonaƒu nɔna ɖeka wɔwɔme kpakple ameyinugbea bena Mawu gã si tso dziƒo la nateŋ akpɔ neneŋ ƒe ameyinugbea ƒe nublanui, eye waoteŋ a hɔɛ ɖe fafaƒe.
ENGLISH: It is a time when the whole family stands together to be in relation with the dead person, and pray for God who comes from heaven to take pity on him, and receive him in peace.

EWE: Esrɔ ɖeɖe le Eʋeawo ƒe dekɔnu wonu.
ENGLISH: Marriage according to Eʋe tradition.

EWE: Le dekɔnua wonu le eʋe dukɔ me la, esrɔɖeɖe nye enu xɔasiaɖe si amewo kãtã tɔna tekpɔ le esime evi nyɔnu lo alo evi ŋtsu ɖo eƒe si dze na esrɔɖeɖe kɔnuwo wɔwɔ.
ENGLISH: According to the tradition of Eʋe population, marriage is an important tradition event that young men and women likely wait for when the rich the age that allow them to participate in this ceremony.

EWE: Le blema kɔnuwo nula, esrɔɖelawo me nyana wonoɛ wo o vaseɖe esime woɖea wonɔɛ wo o.
ENGLISH: With respect to ancient time ceremonies, the lovers do not have to know each other before taking marriage.

EWE: Aleke kɔnuawo va yina enye esi ; ɖevi ŋtsuvila ƒe ƒomea dzina nyɔnuvi si woaɖe la nɛ eye wo dena gbɔme zi etɔ eye emegbe la wo wɔna esrɔ ɖeɖe ƒe kɔnuwo.
ENGLISH: The ceremony goes as follow; the family of the boy will find for him his lover and the family will try to make the family of the girl agree, and this takes few days or month, it depends on each family how the appreciate the offer.

EWE: Aleke wo dea gbɔme ɖoe !ne miagblɛ kpuiɖe ko la, gbɔme dede gɔme enye be woa biata ne nyɔnuvi si ɖegbe ƒomea gbɔna la ne wo ƒe vi ŋtsuvi la.
ENGLISH: The family of the boy has to go to the family of the girl three times according to the tradition to fulfill the marriage ceremony. How it works!

EWE: Zi alesi miegblɔɛ vayi la, gbɔme dede nye enu tɔhɛ si le vevie le esrɔ ɖeɖe ƒe kɔnuwo me.
ENGLISH: To say it shortly, this is the way how the boy’s family ask about marriage to the girl’s family.

EWE: Le kɔnu sia wɔwɔ me la ƒome eveawo dzenasi wonɔɛ wo nyui eye wo danasi ɖe esrɔ ɖeɖe ƒe kɔnuawo dzi.
ENGLISH: In this period the two families try to know each other very well and try to accept each other in sense of allowing the marriage between their children and such period is very important for the whole ceremony.

EWE: Elebe mia dedzesi alesi gbɔme dedea vayina ɖo :
ENGLISH: We generally call this period "knock the door " and will now see his explanation:

EWE: Ametsãtsã tso na ŋtsuvi la ƒe ƒomea me (ŋtsuvila ƒe atagã alo atavi) yina ɖe nyɔnuvi la ƒe ƒomea gbɔ edzi edzi la le fɔfɔ me eye wo ƒoa ʋɔ na nyɔnuvi la ƒe ƒomea eye wo gena ɖe ƒome la ƒe hɔme he doa gbe, eye nyɔnuvi la ƒe ƒomea edzi edzi la nyɔnuvi la ƒe atagã alo atavi hɔna gbe eye biana amaniɛ.
ENGLISH: A chosen people from the boy’s family (generally the uncles of the boy) will go according to the ceremony earlier in the morning to nock to the door of the girl’s family (generally the uncles of the girl) and this people will receive them and ask about the matter.

EWE: Emayi la wo gblɔna na nyɔnuvi la ƒe atagã alo atavi la be yewo dzibe yewoa ɖe wo ƒe vi nyɔnuvi (eye wo yona nyɔnuvi la ƒe ŋko), eye wo tsona aha sɛsɛ atukpã ametɔ (ekuɖe ƒome ɖesiaɖe ƒe dzedze ŋu).
ENGLISH: The boy’s uncles simply reply to the girl’s uncle that they would like to get married with one of their girl (and of course they give the name of the girl) and they give three bottle of alcohol (it depends on every family how much they think is enough).

EWE: Le emayi la Atagã alo atavi si hɔ neneŋ ƒe aha la doa ŋgbe na ɖevi ŋtsuvi la ƒe ƒomea be yeayi ɖa kpɔ nyɔnuvi la ƒe tɔ eye yana nyanya wo kuɖe nyɔnuvi la ƒe tɔ ƒe ɖoɖo ŋti.
ENGLISH: Then the uncle of the girl will let the boy’s uncles know that he will report their intention to the girl’s father and will send then information or propose them another day to come for the answer, it depends.

EWE: Emegbe la ɖevi ŋtsuvi la ƒe ƒomea bia na mɔ eye wo gbugbɔ yina ɖe aƒeme he bɔna amania na ŋtsuvila ƒe tɔ.
ENGLISH: And then the boy’s uncles ask for leaving and go back home to report it to the father of the boy.

EWE: Amesiwo ƒo ʋɔ vayi sã la ga trɔ yina he hɔna ɖoŋti tso nyɔnuvia ƒe tɔ gbɔ (alo nyɔnuvia ƒe atagã alo atavi si hɔ ŋtsuvi la ƒe ƒomeawo vayi la dɔna ame ɖoɖa na ŋtsuvi la ƒe ƒometɔwo kuɖe ɖevi tɔ ƒe lɔlɔ alo gbegbe ŋti.
ENGLISH: The same people from the boy’s family will return again to get the answer from the father of the girl (but sometimes the uncle of the girl can send previously the answer to the boy’s uncles if it is yes or no).

EWE: Ne eva eme be nyɔnuvia ƒe tɔ dasiɖe evia ƒe srɔ ɖeɖe dzila, Ametsãtsã tso ŋtsuvi la ƒe ƒomeame ga gbugbɔ trɔ yina nyɔnuvila ƒe atagã alo atavi gbɔ he sena enusiwo woadi va hena nyɔnuvila ƒe ɖeɖe.
ENGLISH: If it is happen that the girl’s father says yes, the same people from the boy’s family return back again to hear about their duties concerning the marriage of the girl and their son.

EWE: Enusiwo woa heva la vayi na ale : aha (aha vivi, aha sɛsɛ, todzi ha, deha kple bubuwo… kple wo ƒe home neni), avɔ ɖaka (tsigãvɔ, holãdvɔ, tsivivɔ, keŋte, sika gavi kple awle, dzonu kle bubuwo…), ega (nyɔnuvi la ƒe ƒomea nana kpɔɖeŋ, akpaɖe yina na nyɔnuvia ƒe tɔ eye akpaɖe yina na nyɔnuvia hã) kple susu be nyɔnuvia megaɖu aya o, edze (ekuɖe ƒome ɖesiaɖeŋ), kple enu bubu wo sɔŋ……
ENGLISH: An example of their duties; drinks (soft drinks, alcohols for example local one like SOƉABI or from abroad like gins, palm wine etc…), cloth (like special home cloth for example loin cloth, wax Hollanders etc.. with some specific quantities, jewelry and so on), money (the girl’s family gives some specific amount, the minimum, some part goes to the family and another part goes to the girl in intention that the girl can start doing business with this money and be safe from hunger), salt (it depend on each family, the will spend this salt in the family and close relation to let them know that their girl get married), and many other things…..

EWE: Ne ŋtsuvila ƒe ƒomea ƒle enusiawo kãtã vɔ la, wo dɔna amedɔdɔ ɖoɖa nyɔnuvi la ƒe ƒomea eye wo ɖona ŋkeke si dzi woava ahe enuawo vɛ, eye woa wo nyɔnuvila ƒe ɖeɖe ƒe kɔnuwo.
ENGLISH: When the boy’s family is ready (means they buy every think), they will send information to the girl’s family that they would like to come and fulfill their duties to get into the marriage ceremony.

EWE: Elebe mia do dzesi be le eyiyi siawo kãtã mela, le tsã hoho ƒe game la, ŋtsuvila kple nyɔnuvila menya na wonɔɛwo o, wɔ gaɖome la ameaɖewo fina tofi na ŋtsuvila alo nyɔnuvila, eya nyena wodada eye woateŋ ahe tona nɛnɛŋ ƒe amewo ne wo dzesi wo.
ENGLISH: We have to notice that in the pass the lovers do not know each other during this period of consultation, but sometimes some people let the boy or the girl know about the information and this bad intention and those people can be punished if their recognized by the families involve in the ceremony.

EWE: Esrɔ ɖeɖe nye enu tohɛ aɖe le blema me ale be evi ƒomea ye tsana ŋgbetɔ srɔ na wo ƒe vi, kple susu be wo ƒe vi mega kpefu le esrɔ ɖeɖe gome wo.
ENGLISH: Why that simply because the girl or the boy can run away from their family if they don’t want get married.

EWE: Ne ŋkeke dzi va ɖo la, ŋtsuvila ƒe ƒomea kplɔna ɖekakpuila ɖe asi he tsɔna enusiwo wo ƒle hena srɔ ɖeɖe ƒe kɔnuawo la ɖe asi heyina ɖe ɖetugbuila ƒe ƒomea gbɔɛ.
ENGLISH: Marriage was very important in the pass according to Eʋe tradition in sense that it is the family that chooses the partner for their son or daughter in fear that the boy or girl will not suffer or have difficult life.

EWE: Afima ye ɖekakpuila kple ɖetugbuila dzenasi wonɔɛwo le abe ŋgbetɔ srɔ.
ENGLISH: It will be the time when the lovers will officially discover their partner for life.

EWE: Kɔnuawo vayina ale ; nuƒo tɔhɛ tso ƒome eveawo me kple yrayrawo, kple dzidzɔ kpɔkpɔwo, kple enunonowo, kple eʋu ƒoƒowo, ewoe ɖuɖuwo kpakple vividodoɖe srɔɖelawo ŋti vayi edzi nyuie.
ENGLISH: The ceremony goes as follow: some special speech come from the both family with happiness, with drinking times, with the sound of drams, with special dancing times with appreciation of the couple and so on…

EWE: Elebe mia ɖo ŋku edzibe, gaɖewo mela, ɖekakpuila kple ɖetugbuila me teŋ doa dzidzɔ ɖe wonoɛ wo ŋti o, elabena menye wo dzidzi be yewoa ɖe amesi wotsã na yewo la o, vɔa womateŋ awɔ naɖeke si ƒomea medasiɖo o.
ENGLISH: Here we have to know that sometimes it is difficult for the couple to enjoy this time because it happen that they do not like each other, but nevertheless, they have to show that their happy because of their parents.

EWE: Le kɔnuawo ƒe dziyiyi me la, ɖetugbuila ƒe tɔ lena ɖetugbuila ƒe alɔ he dena ɖekakpuila ƒe ƒomea si tɔhɛɖe he gblɔna be, me tsɔ nye ɖetugbuila de asina mi, mialebenɛ nyui eye mia kpɔ etadzi nyui bena mega ɖu aya o, alo mego kpefu o, eye wo gblɔna be ɛ mia lebenɛ eye mia kpɔ etadzi nyui.
ENGLISH: When the ceremony is still on, the girl’s father takes her hand and gives her to the boy’s family and says for example, I give you my daughter; you have to take care of her that she will never suffer from hunger or will not have difficult life and they will say yes we will take care of her and give her better life.

EWE: Le enuwuwu la, ɖekakpuila ƒe ƒomea kplɔna ɖetugbuila yina ɖe woɖokui wogbɔ he tsɔɛ dasina ɖekakpuila.
ENGLISH: And at the end the boy’s family come home with the girl and gives her to the boy.

EWE: Esrɔɖeɖe ƒe kɔnu sia nye kɔnu si amewo lebena nyuie le blemame, wɔa gake le egbeƒe ŋkekea wo mela, amewo mega dena bubu neneŋ ƒe kɔnuwo nu o.
ENGLISH: (About the virginity of the girl is very important from the boy’s family but nevertheless I am not going deeply about this fact here).

EWE: Amewo le srɔɖem le egbeƒe ŋkekea wo me le mɔdododzi, le ʋuƒoƒewo, le esetɔwogbɔ, le tsɔtsihɔme kple afi bubuwo sike evi ƒomea mega nyena amesi tsãna ŋgbetɔsrɔ o, keboŋ ɖe efu domoɖa la, hafi wonyana.
ENGLISH: People take care of this marriage ceremony in pass, but these days’ people do not respect this marriage ceremony.

EWE: Wɔa, ameaɖeo gakpɔtɔ le neneŋ ƒe blema kɔnuwo meɖe asi, eye wonɔ edzi yim nenema, amedzro aɖeo hã vana va wɔna esrɔ ɖeɖe le Eʋeawo ƒe dekɔnu wonu he gblɔna be enye enu tɔhɛ na yewo eye wo trɔ dzona.
ENGLISH: People taking these days marriage everywhere without parents acceptance, people meet each other on road, in pub, dram music places decide about marriage without parents intervention, taking marriage only with regard with the law, in church and other places.

EWE: Mekã alesi ŋgbetɔsrɔawo kpɔ wonɔɛ woɖo alo afisi wowɔ srɔɖeɖe ƒe kɔnuwo le o, elebe ɖekakpuila na nya ɖetugbuila ƒe ƒomea eye woa degbɔme na ɖetugbuila hena eƒeta biabia le eƒe ƒomea gbɔ, ele vevie.
ENGLISH: But we must notice that a lot of people still in respect with ancient time marriage ceremonies, and some foreign people come sometimes specially in taking part in this traditional marriage and go back to their country because the fill special after all.

EWE: Ne ɖekakpuila mewɔ eta biabia kɔnuawo o la, ne eva dzɔ be ɖetugbuila ƒe ƒomea ƒe ameɖeku alo ɖetugbuila kula, elenebe woawɔ eta biabia kɔnuawo hafi woaɖemɔnɛ be woakpɔ amekukula alo woageɖe ɖetugbuila ƒe ƒomea me le seanu.
ENGLISH: No matter where the lovers find themselves or where they get married, the boy must find out the girl’s family and fulfill his duties about traditional married, it is very important in Eʋe tradition.

EWE: Tɔgbe nye ŋkɔ enye AFOUTOU Kodjovi Akpan, enye ame dzɛ aɖe si tso Tado, teƒe si le ɣedzepe godzi eye wo nye ame dzesi aɖe le Tado-Domé.
ENGLISH: If not, and it happens that the member of the girl’s family died or the girl’s herself died, before this boy will be receive officially by his step-family he has to fulfill this marriage ceremony entirely according to the tradition and it complicated because he has to fulfill more duties.

EWE: Kpui ɖe ko la, enye vodu nɔ gã aɖe tsã vayi, si ɖo vodu hapopo si wɔa kɔnu vovovowo eye dukɔa kãtã nyɛ nɛ.
ENGLISH: The name of my grandfather is Kodjovi Akpa Afoutou, with clear complexion skin; he is a known person from Tado-Domé which located at the East-South side of the country.

EWE: Eda gbe le ame ŋti eye wo poanu kuɖe amegbetɔ ƒe kuɣɛwo ŋti alo eƒe esɔme ŋti alo eƒe vivime ŋti.
ENGLISH: Shortly, he was animist and had a group of people who worship "Vodu " and who can cure disease, speak about people problem and can read things in future.

EWE: Ekpa eha vovovowo ɣe doa eƒe vodu la ƒe ŋkɔ ɖedzi eye le woƒe kɔnu wɔwɔ eyiyi hã.
ENGLISH: He has composed many songs to glorify « Vodu » and as well during ceremonies for the same purpose.

EWE: Enɔ esia dzi vasɛɖe esime wo trɔ dzime zu Katoliko hɔsetɔ vãvã.
ENGLISH: He had been doing this till he seriously converted into Catholicism.

EWE: Etrɔ dzime alegbegbe be egbe nu le abosãŋ kple eƒe nuwɔna vovovowo gbɔ.
ENGLISH: He was truly converted that he finished everything with Satan and its duties.

EWE: Ekpa eha geɖe na Mawu ƒe ŋkɔ dodoɖedzi eye amewo dzina neneŋ ƒe eha wo le tsotsi hɔ alo gbedohɔ me ɣena vivi dodoɖe subɔ subɔ ɖe Mawu ŋti.
ENGLISH: He started compose songs for worshiping God and those song were sung in Church by people to glorify God during the celebration of Mass.

EWE: Amewo nya eƒe hawo ale gbegbe be esi Papa Yohanes Paolo ewe lia va Togo le eƒe akpe ɖeka bla sieke kple enyiʋɔ atɔ le ɣleti enyi lia me (08/1985) la, wo yɔɛ be wɔa va dziha nɛ le eƒe misa me, eye emegbe la eyi Papa gbɔ va dziha nɛ.
ENGLISH: People knew his songs and they were useful for the Mass that they invited him to sing during the celebration of Mass when Pope John II came to Togo in August 1985, and then after the Mass he went to sing for Pope.

EWE: Edze be ma ɖo ŋku edzi be, le eyiyi ma wome la fada ameve tso Polonyi nɔ Tado-Domé ƒe katoliko hanɔƒea.
ENGLISH: I have to mention that, at that time we have in our village Tado-Domé, two Priests from Poland who were catholic missionaries.

EWE: Eƒe eha vevi dometɔ ɖeka enye « Mawu nya vivi » eye eha ƒe eme nyawo enye :
ENGLISH: One of his best songs was "God’s words are sweet " and the song’s words were:

EWE: Mawu nya vivi
ENGLISH: God’s words are sweet

EWE: Akpan be mawu nya vivi ŋtɔ (2x)
ENGLISH: Akpan says God’s words are too sweet

EWE: Ameɖe gbe Mawu nya ŋdi kɛnyɛ
ENGLISH: Somebody refuse the word in morning

EWE: Fiɛ sime ɖo afoku la va dzedzie (2x)
ENGLISH: In evening he will meet trouble (or accident)

EWE: chorus:
ENGLISH: chorus:

EWE: Edze vivinɔ
ENGLISH: Salt is sweet

EWE: Ɣehowa be edze vivinɔ
ENGLISH: Yehowa says salt is sweet

EWE: Dzeɖe gbebe eye ma vivivo
ENGLISH: The salt that refuse to be sweet

EWE: Ye woa sɔ kɔŋgbe aso afo so lidzi.
ENGLISH: It will be throwing away and walk over.

EWE: Ŋkɔ nye enye AFOUTOU Djoubogbé Kossi, o dzim le damɛ ŋkeke blawe vɔ ene, le eƒe akpe ɖeka alafa asieke blanyi vɔ ɖekɛ lia dzi(24/05/1981).
ENGLISH: My name is AFOUTOU Djoubogbé Kossi, I was born in May 24, 1981.

EWE: Etɔnye ŋkɔ enye Kounoudji etso Tado-Domé (Moyen-Mono) eye enɔnye ŋkɔ enye Akouvi tso Kouma-Aɖamé (Kloto nuto me).
ENGLISH: My father’s name is Kounoudzi from Tado-Domé (Moyen-Mono) and my mother’s name is Akouvi from Kouma-Aɖamé (Kloto).

EWE: Meɖo nɔvi nyɔnuvi eve kple nɔvi ŋsuvi eve.
ENGLISH: I have two sisters and two brothers.

EWE: Mewu nye suku nu le « Université de Lomé » eye me hɔ diplom si ŋkɔ enye « Maîtrise en Gestion » le efe akpe eve kple adɛ me(2006).
ENGLISH: I was graduated at University of Lomé and I had master in "Accounting, Business Administration and Management " in 2006.

EWE: Meva Polonyi zi gbãtɔ le eƒe akpe eve kple adrɛ lia me (2007) to AIESEC ƒe ɖoɖo nu, na enu fiafia kuɖe akɔta kple adzɔ dodo nya wo ŋti le polonyi ƒe suku kɔkɔ wo si ŋkɔ nye « szkoła średnia » le Wielkopolska ƒenu towo me.
ENGLISH: I came to Poland for the first time in 2007 for an internship through AIESEC in teaching entrepreneurship and culture in Wielkopolska region’s high schools.

EWE: Le eyiyi ma me la, mekpo be monu kpokpo le ŋtinye, be mateŋ ade suku kɔkɔ lafiyi.
ENGLISH: At this time I notice that it is an opportunity for me to study here.

EWE: Eye esi metrɔ yi Togo le ɣleti gbãto ƒe ŋkeke wiatɔ liadzi le eƒe akpe eve kple enyi la me la (15/01/2008), me tamɔ be ma va yi suku nye dzi le afiyi (Poznan), elabena suku fɛa me sɔgbɔ la fiyi o, eye medi hã vevie be ma de sukua le aɣlisigbeme.
ENGLISH: And when I return back to Togo in January 15, 2008 I plan to continuous my studies here (in Poznan), because the tuition fee is cheaper and I wanted as well to study in English.

EWE: Metrɔwa Polonyi le dasiamime ŋkeke wiatɔ liadzi le eƒe akpe eve kple enyi liadzi (15/08/2008) vaseɖe ŋkeke sia dzi.
ENGLISH: I came back in August 15, 2008 till today.

EWE: Menye ɖekakpui aɖe si dzina dzɔdzɔɛ nye nye, anukɔɖe kple ŋtifafa eye me wɔdɔ vevie elabena me kãɖedzi be edɔwɔwɔ ɖeka ko ateŋ a ɣe vovo va na ame siame.
ENGLISH: I am a gentleman who fights for justice, truth and peace and I work hard because I believe that only real work can bring freedom to everybody.

EWE: Nye dzidzi enye be ma trɔ ŋɖe le hehe ya me, ma ʋli ŋtifafa eye ma kpeɖe wɔamenɔ kple fukpelawo ŋti.
ENGLISH: My ambition is to change something in this world, fight for peace and help poor and suffering people.

EWE: Taɖodzi nye enye be ma wɔdɔ eye emegbe la, ma ʋu nye ŋtɔ ƒe adzɔ nu le esɔ me.
ENGLISH: My target is first to work for company and open my own business in the future.

EWE: Eye nye ŋkɔ ƒoɖo nya enye be "Afrika dukɔwo ɣia vovo kpokpo ".
ENGLISH: And my motto is "African countries want to be free ".

EWE: KƆSIƉAME ŊKEKEWO KPLE EME NYAWO
ENGLISH: DAYS IN THE WEEK WITH THEIR STEREOTIPES

EWE: Le Eʋe dukɔwo mela, ŋkɔ nye dzesiaɖe, eye dzigbe ŋkeke nyena ŋkeke tɔxɛ na Eʋevi ɖesiaɖe klui.
ENGLISH: Mean while almost every person from Ewe group is named according to the day in the week on which he or she was born.

EWE: Tso Dzoɖa ŋkekedzi vasede Kɔsiɖa ƒe ŋkekedzi la, ŋkeke ɖesiaɖe ɖo dzigbe ƒe ŋkɔ, eye neneŋ ƒe ŋkɔ ɖena amesi tsɔ ŋkɔla ƒe aƒevi nyenye fiana.
ENGLISH: And it easy to remember the day in the week on which one person was born, because each day in the week has a specific name, which is connected with Ewe culture.

EWE: Dzigbezã alo dzigbe ŋkɔ ateŋ aƒonu kuɖe amesi tsɔ ŋkɔla ƒe tsɔme ŋti.
ENGLISH: The person using one of those names are easily identify as Ewe ethnical group descendant.

EWE: Miele nu ŋlɔge tso neneŋ ƒe ŋkɔ kple eƒe tsɔme nyawo ŋti le enyasio gbɔna la me :
ENGLISH: We are going to provide information about the names, their meaning and their stereotype in the coming words:

EWE: DZOƉA: ŋkeke gbãtɔ - dzoɖaviwo
ENGLISH: MONDAY: Day one – Monday’s natives

EWE: Emevio tɔna ŋkɔ siawo :
ENGLISH: Descendant from Ewe group named as follow:

EWE: Ŋsuwo : Kɔdzo, Kɔdzo, Kɔdzovi, Kɔdzogã, Kudzo, Kudzovi, Kudzogã
ENGLISH: Boys: Kɔdzo, Kɔdzo, Kɔdzovi, Kɔdzogã, Kudzo, Kudzovi, Kudzogã

EWE: Nyɔnuwo : Adzo, Adzovi, Adzogã, Adzowavi, Adzowagã, Adzowa, Adzotɔ.
ENGLISH: Girls: Adzo, Adzovi, Adzogã, Adzowavi, Adzowagã, Adzowa, Adzotɔ.

EWE: Dzoɖaviwo ƒe agbeme wɔnawo kple woƒe nunana tso wɔla gbɔ Dzoɖaviwo nye na amefafa wo, wo me ʋlinaɖo kaba kaba le enuwo ŋti o, vɔ gake to egbɔ be woateŋ a tsidzi hã la, wo buna tame ŋtɔ hafi wo wɔnanu.
ENGLISH: Life style of Monday’s natives and their spirit gift from the creator Monday’s natives are generally shy, they do not hurry much about things, even though they could, they do think over before taken appropriate action according to the situation.

EWE: Dzoɖaviwo me lɔnabe yewoa dzagɔ le amedzi o, eye wo haanu alegbegbe nenye be wo wɔnu davo le amebubu ŋti.
ENGLISH: They do not like to offend or hurt people and they suffer if it happens that they do hurt or make other people sad.

EWE: Dzoɖaviwo lɔna ame vevie eye wo tsɔnanu doadzidzɔ ɖe woƒe ameveviewo alo woƒe lɔlɔtɔwo ŋti, wo dzina hã be amewo nelɔ yewo abe yewo lɔwo ene, eye ameɖokui tsɔtsɔ savɔ ɖe amebubuta nyena dzoɖavio ƒe agbemenyawo.
ENGLISH: Monday’s natives are people who love very much their partner or their friends and they like to offer gift to their close relations or partner to make them happy, they want people to like or love them the same way they did to them, and they easily can offer their life to save others.

EWE: Lɔlɔ nye nu tɔhɛ na wo.
ENGLISH: Love is very important for them.

EWE: Dzoɖaviwo dzina be yewoa wɔ nugãwo le agbeme eye wo nɔna drɔɛgãwo kukum, wo ga nyena amesiwo nɔna dzikudom edzi edzi eye le eyiyiaɖewo megbe kola, wobe dziku dodoa nu va yina enumake.
ENGLISH: They like to make great realizations and they do have great dreams, also they are people that quickly become angry and after few time they become happy.

EWE: BRAƉA: ŋkeke evelia – braɖaviwo
ENGLISH: TUESDAY: Day two – Tuesday’s natives

EWE: Emevio tɔna ŋkɔ siawo :
ENGLISH: Descendant from Ewe group named as follow:

EWE: Ŋsuwo : Kɔmla, Kɔmlavi, Kɔmlagã
ENGLISH: Boys: Kɔmla, Kɔmlavi, Kɔmlagã

EWE: Nyɔnuwo : Abra, Abravi, Abragã, Abrewavi, Abrewagã, Abrewa
ENGLISH: Girls: Abra, Abravi, Abragã, Abrewavi, Abrewagã, Abrewa

EWE: Braɖaviwo ƒe agbeme wɔnawo kple woƒe nunana tso wɔla gbɔ Braɖaviwo nyena amesiwo nyananu kuɖe amegbetɔ ƒomea ŋti.
ENGLISH: Life style of Tuesday’s natives and their spirit gift from the creator Tuesday’s natives, are people that have a great gift of general over view about humans, they know humans characteristics well.

EWE: Wo ga nyena amesiwo kpɔna dzidzɔ alo wɔna vividodoɖe amehaviwo ŋti.
ENGLISH: They like to enjoy themselves and their relations.

EWE: Nublanui kpɔkpɔɖe amehaviwo ŋti nyena enusi hɔna teƒe geɖe le woƒe agbewome.
ENGLISH: They like to express their feelings to people, and they can use their time or moment doing so.

EWE: Braɖaviwo ɖoato amewo nyuie, woƒe nugɔmesese nye kpɔɖeŋu eye le nenemanu ke woƒe dziku dodo kaba kaba hã vaname ema.
ENGLISH: They like to be close and listen to people, their understanding is an example but in the same way they become quickly angry.

EWE: Braɖaviwo nye amesiwo lɔnabe yewoa nye amekplɔlawo alo zimenɔlawo alo amenunɔlawo.
ENGLISH: They like to be leader or chief or responsible for something.

EWE: Braɖaviwo kpɔna dzidzɔ alegbegbe eye tamesusu nyuie hã nɔna wosi alebe enuenula, wo dzinabe yewoa wɔ nusi dze alo nusi nye nuteƒe la.
ENGLISH: They are happy people and they do have very great mind mean while they are rational people and they do things true.

EWE: Braɖaviwo nyena amesiwo nyananu nyuie eye woƒe nusɔsrɔ wɔnawo le suku dzenaedzi nawo nyuie alegbegbebe, edɔwɔwɔ kude agbãle ŋti alo asinu dɔwɔwɔ nye enusi ɖenavi nawo ŋtɔ.
ENGLISH: The natives of Tuesday are intelligent people, they observe great studying and the have success in professional life.

EWE: Braɖaviwo lɔna enumama kple wohaviwo eye wo ɖona enukomo ɖe wohaviwo ŋti.
ENGLISH: They like to share and welcome people.

EWE: KUƉA: ŋkeke etɔlia – kuɖaviwo
ENGLISH: WEDNESDAY: Day three – Wednesday’s natives

EWE: Eme vio tɔna ŋkɔ siawo :
ENGLISH: Descendant from Ewe group named as follow:

EWE: Ŋsuwo : Kɔku, Kɔkuvi, Kɔkugã
ENGLISH: Boys: Kɔku, Kɔkuvi, Kɔkugã

EWE: Susuŋutinunyala Aɖe Ƒe Xɔse
ENGLISH: A Brain Pathologist Explains His Faith

EWE: NUFIALAGÃ Rajesh Kalaria, si le Newcastle Yunivɛsiti le England la le nu srɔ̃m tso amegbetɔwo ƒe susu ŋu wu ƒe 40.
ENGLISH: PROFESSOR Rajesh Kalaria, of Newcastle University, England, has studied the human brain for more than 40 years.

EWE: Tsãa, exɔe se be ɖe nuwo dzɔ le wo ɖokui si.
ENGLISH: He used to believe in evolution.

EWE: Gake eva trɔ susu emegbe.
ENGLISH: But later, he changed his views.

EWE: Nyɔ! magazinea talawo bia gbee tso eƒe xɔse kpakple eƒe dɔa ŋu.
ENGLISH: Awake! asked him about his work and faith.

EWE: Míeɖe kuku subɔsubɔha ka mee nènɔ tsã?
ENGLISH: Please tell us about your religious background.

EWE: Wodzi tɔnye le India, eye togbɔ be Indiatɔe danye nye hã Uganda ye wodzii le.
ENGLISH: My father was born in India, and my mother, although of Indian origin, was born in Uganda.

EWE: Hindutɔwo ƒe dzixɔsewo koŋue kpɔ ŋusẽ ɖe wo dzi.
ENGLISH: Their lives were largely governed by Hindu customs.

EWE: Mí ame etɔ̃e wodzi eye nyee nye evelia.
ENGLISH: I am the second of three children.

EWE: Míenɔ Nairobi, le Kenya.
ENGLISH: We lived in Nairobi, Kenya.

EWE: Hindutɔ geɖewo hã nɔ afi ma.
ENGLISH: Many other Hindu people lived nearby.

EWE: Nu kae na dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunya va dzɔ dzi na wò?
ENGLISH: What stimulated your interest in science?

EWE: Lãwo ƒe nu dzɔa dzi nam eye zi geɖe la, nye kple xɔ̃nyewo míezɔa mɔ legbeewo ɖatsia avewo me be míakpɔ lãwo.
ENGLISH: I was always interested in animals, and I often went hiking and camping with my friends to see the spectacular wildlife.

EWE: Dɔ si koŋ medi be mawɔe nye be manye lãwo ƒe ɖɔkta.
ENGLISH: My initial goal was to be a veterinary surgeon.

EWE: Gake esi medo le asinudɔsrɔ̃suku aɖe le Nairobi la, meyi London Yunivɛsiti le England, va srɔ̃ nu tso ale si dɔlékuiwo wɔna tsina ŋu.
ENGLISH: But after graduating from a technical college in Nairobi, I went to England to study pathology at the University of London.

EWE: Emegbe meva srɔ̃ nu tso amegbetɔwo ƒe ahɔhɔ̃ koŋ ŋu.
ENGLISH: Later, I specialized in research into the human brain.

EWE: Ðe wò sukunusɔsrɔ̃wo kpɔ ŋusẽ ɖe wò dzixɔsewo dzia?
ENGLISH: Did your studies affect your religious beliefs?
Yes.

EWE: Esi menɔ nu geɖe srɔ̃m tso dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunya ŋu la, eva sesẽ nam be mayi edzi axɔ Hindutɔwo ƒe nyakpakpawo kple kɔnuwo dzi ase.
ENGLISH: The more I studied science, the harder I found it to believe in Hindu mythology and traditions, such as the worship of animals and images.

EWE: Esia ƒe ɖewoe nye lãwo kple legbawo subɔsubɔ.
ENGLISH: Why did you accept the teaching of evolution?

EWE: Esi menye ɖevi la, ame siwo dome menɔ la xɔe se be Afrika ye nɔnɔmetɔtrɔ dze egɔme tsoe, eye wofiaa nu siawo mí le suku enuenu.
ENGLISH: In my younger years, many people around me held the view that human evolution began in Africa, and we often discussed this idea at school.

EWE: Azɔ hã, nufialawo kple yunivɛsiti nufialagãwo na mí sukuviawo míexɔe se be dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyala gãwo katã ka ɖe edzi be ɖe nuwo dzɔ le wo ɖokui si.
ENGLISH: Also, the teachers and university professors gave us students the impression that all respected scientists believe in evolution.

EWE: Esi ɣeyiɣiawo va nɔ yiyim la, wò susu va trɔ le afi si agbe dzɔ tso ŋu.
ENGLISH: In time you reconsidered the question of the origin of life.

EWE: Nu ka tae?
ENGLISH: Why?

EWE: Menɔ nu srɔ̃m tso nu gbagbewo kple woƒe wɔwɔme ŋu ƒe aɖewo va se ɖe esime sukuhati aɖe va gblɔ nu siwo srɔ̃m wònɔ le Biblia me tso Yehowa Ðasefowo gbɔ la nam.
ENGLISH: I had been studying biology and anatomy for some years when a fellow student told me what he was learning about the Bible from Jehovah’s Witnesses.

EWE: Medi be manya nu geɖe.
ENGLISH: I became curious.

EWE: Eya ta esi Ðasefoawo va wɔ takpekpe aɖe le míaƒe sukua ƒe takpexɔ me le Nairobi la, nye hã mede.
ENGLISH: So when the Witnesses held an assembly at our college hall in Nairobi, I attended.

EWE: Emegbe Ðasefo eve siwo nye dutanyanyuigblɔlawo va ɖe Biblia me nufiafia aɖewo me nam.
ENGLISH: Later, two Witness missionaries explained some Bible teachings to me.

EWE: Esi mekpɔe be woxɔ Wɔla Gã aɖe dzi se eye be egbɔe míakpɔ agbemebiabia vevitɔwo ƒe ŋuɖoɖowo le la, nyemebui kura be nyakpakpa aɖee o.
ENGLISH: Their belief in a Grand Designer who has the answers to life’s big questions did not sound like mythology.

EWE: Enya se nam eye susu le eme hã.
ENGLISH: It appealed to me as being reasonable.

EWE: Ðe nu siwo nèsrɔ̃ tso ahɔhɔ̃a ŋu na wòsesẽ na wò be nàxɔe ase be ɖe wowɔ nuwoa?
ENGLISH: Did your medical knowledge hinder your belief in creation?

EWE: Kura o!
ENGLISH: On the contrary!

EWE: Esi menɔ nu srɔ̃m tso nuwo ƒe wɔwɔme ŋu la, meva kpɔe be wowɔ nu gbagbewo le mɔ wɔnuku aɖe ŋutɔ nu.
ENGLISH: As I studied anatomy, I saw how well-designed and complex living things are.

EWE: Be míagblɔ be naneke mefiaa mɔ nuwɔwɔ wɔnuku siawo o la nye nu si me susu megava nɔ nam o.
ENGLISH: To attribute such a high level of sophistication to an unguided process no longer made sense to me.

EWE: Àte ŋu agblɔ eƒe kpɔɖeŋu aɖe na mía?
ENGLISH: Can you give us an example?

EWE: Medze nusɔsrɔ̃ tso amegbetɔ ƒe ahɔhɔ̃ ŋu tso ƒe 1970-awo me, eye ahɔhɔ̃a ƒe dɔwɔwɔ gawɔa nuku nam kokoko.
ENGLISH: I have studied the human brain since the early 1970’s, and this remarkable organ never ceases to amaze me.

EWE: Ahɔhɔ̃a koŋ ye nana míebua tame, ɖoa ŋku nu dzi eye wònana míaƒe ŋutinu vovovoawo katã wɔa dɔ.
ENGLISH: It is the seat of thought and memory and the control center for many bodily functions.

EWE: Eya kee nana lãmesidzenu vovovoawo wɔa dɔ eye wòwɔa nyatakaka siwo tso ametia me kple esiwo tso ametia godo siaa ŋu dɔ.
ENGLISH: The brain is also the hub of our many senses, interpreting information that comes from both inside and outside the body.

EWE: Susu si ta míaƒe ahɔhɔ̃a wɔa dɔ nyuie nye be eme tsiwo kple ahɔhɔ̃menugbagbeviwo wɔa dɔ aduadu le mɔ wɔnuku aɖe nu.
ENGLISH: Our brain functions the way it does largely because of its complex chemistry and intricate networks of neurons, the primary brain cells.

EWE: Ahɔhɔ̃menugbagbevi biliɔn gbogbo aɖewoe le amegbetɔ ƒe ahɔhɔ̃ me, eye wowɔa dɔ aduadu kple wo nɔewo to lãmeka falɛfalɛ legbee siwo woyɔna le Eŋlisigbe me be axons dzi.
ENGLISH: The human brain has many billions of neurons, which communicate with one another through long fibers called axons.

EWE: Ahɔhɔ̃menugbagbevi siawo dometɔ ɖeka ate ŋu awɔ dɔ aduadu kple ahɔhɔ̃menugbagbevi bubuwo to lãmeka falɛfalɛ (dendrites) siwo dzea alɔ la dzi.
ENGLISH: From these, a single neuron may make many thousands of connections with other neurons by way of branching fibers called dendrites.

EWE: Esia wɔe be xexlẽme mele ale si ahɔhɔ̃mekawo de nu wo nɔewo me ŋu o!
ENGLISH: As a result, the total number of connections in the brain is astronomical!

EWE: Azɔ hã ahɔhɔ̃menugbagbevi akpeakpe siawo kple lãmeka falɛfalɛ siawo wɔa dɔ ɖe ɖoɖo nyui nu eye wometɔtɔna o.
ENGLISH: What is more, this dense forest of neurons and dendrites is, not chaotic, but precise.

EWE: Ale si "wolɔ̃ " ɖe wo nɔewo me la wɔ nuku ŋutɔ.
ENGLISH: It is an amazing feat of "wiring. "

EWE: Míeɖe kuku ɖe eme.
ENGLISH: Please explain.

EWE: Ahɔhɔ̃mekawo dzea dɔwɔwɔ ɖe ɖoɖo nu gɔme ne vidzĩwo le dɔ me kple ne wodzi wo vɔ megbe.
ENGLISH: The wiring progresses in a most orderly way during a baby’s development in the womb as well as postnatally.

EWE: Ahɔhɔ̃menugbagbeviwo ɖoa lãmeka falɛfalɛwo ɖa be woavae tsiã kple ahɔhɔ̃menugbagbevi bubu siwo dome didi tso wo gbɔ sentimeta ʋɛ aɖewo gake dometsotsoa adidi ŋutɔ ne lãmenugbagbeviwo gbɔe woɖo wo ɖo.
ENGLISH: Neurons send out fibers to target neurons that may be a few centimeters away​ a vast distance on the cellular level.

EWE: Gake menye lãmenugbagbevi aɖe koŋ koe lãmeka falɛfalɛa yina ɖatsiãna kple o ke eƒe akpa aɖe koŋ ye.
ENGLISH: The target of a fiber, by the way, may be not just a specific cell but a specific part of that cell.

EWE: Ne lãmeka falɛfalɛ yeye aɖe dze tso ahɔhɔ̃meka aɖe me la, lãmetsiwo fiaa mɔe eye wogblɔna nɛ be "tɔ, " "dzo " alo "trɔ " va se ɖe esime wòaɖo afi si yim wòle.
ENGLISH: As a new fiber branches out from a neuron, it is guided by chemical signposts that say such things as "stop, " "go, " or "turn " until the fiber reaches its target.

EWE: Ne womefia mɔ lãmeka falɛfalɛ siawo nyuie o la, woabu.
ENGLISH: Without clear instructions, growing fibers would soon get lost.

EWE: Ale si nu siawo katã wɔa dɔ nukutɔe la nɔ te ɖe mɔfiame siwo woŋlɔ ɖe domenyiŋusẽfianua (DNA, ADN) me la dzi.
ENGLISH: The whole process is brilliantly orchestrated, starting with the instructions written in our DNA.

EWE: Togbɔ be míenya nu siawo hã la, nu gbogbo aɖewo gali siwo mímenya tso ale si ahɔhɔ̃a wɔa dɔe, ale si wòwɔna ɖoa ŋku nu dzi, ɖea seselelãmewo fiana kple ale si wòbua nuwo ŋu la nyuie o.
ENGLISH: That said, we are far from understanding fully how the brain develops and functions, including how it forms memories, emotions, and thoughts.

EWE: Le gonyeme la, ale si ahɔhɔ̃a wɔa dɔe ɖeɖe dzaa fiam be ame aɖe si ƒe susu de ŋgɔ sãsãsã wu mía tɔ la li, eye mehiã be maƒo nu tso ale si ahɔhɔ̃a wɔa dɔe tsitotsito gɔ̃ hã ŋu o.
ENGLISH: For me, just the fact that the brain works​ not to mention how well it works and how beautifully it develops ​points to a mind far superior to our own.

EWE: Nu kae na nèva zu Yehowa Ðasefo?
ENGLISH: Why did you become one of Jehovah’s Witnesses?

EWE: Ðasefoawo na mekpɔ kpeɖodziwo be Biblia nye Mawu ƒe Nya.
ENGLISH: The Witnesses showed me evidence that the Bible is God’s Word.

EWE: Le kpɔɖeŋu me, menye dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyagbalẽe Biblia nye o, gake ne ele nu ƒom tso dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunya ŋu la edena pɛpɛpɛ.
ENGLISH: For example, the Bible is not a science book, but when it touches on scientific matters, it is consistently correct.

EWE: Nyagblɔɖi siwo de pɛpɛpɛ hã le eme.
ENGLISH: It also contains accurate prophecies.

EWE: Eye ame siwo wɔna ɖe emenyawo dzi la nɔa agbe nyui.
ENGLISH: And it improves the lives of those who apply its teachings.

EWE: Ale si mele agbe nɔm fifia la hã nye kpeɖodzi ɖeka.
ENGLISH: My own life is evidence of that.

EWE: Tso esime meva zu Yehowa Ðasefo le ƒe 1973 me la, Bibliae nye agbalẽ vevitɔ si fiaa mɔm.
ENGLISH: Since I became one of Jehovah’s Witnesses in 1973, the Bible has been my guidebook.

EWE: Esia wɔe be nye dzi dze eme eye taɖodzinu va le nye agbe ŋu.
ENGLISH: As a result, my life has become truly satisfying and purposeful.

EWE: Fugboeŋutinunyala Aɖe Ƒe Xɔse
ENGLISH: An Embryologist Explains His Faith

EWE: NUFIALAGÃ Yan-Der Hsuuw nye fugboewo ŋuti nusrɔ̃ƒe dzi kpɔla le Taiwantɔwo ƒe yunivɛsiti aɖe me.
ENGLISH: PROFESSOR Yan-Der Hsuuw is the director of embryo research at Taiwan’s National Pingtung University of Science and Technology.

EWE: Tsã la, exɔ amedzɔtsolãme ƒe nufiafiaa dzi se, gake esi wòva zu dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyala si wɔa numekuku la, etrɔ susu.
ENGLISH: He once believed in evolution, but after becoming a research scientist, he changed his mind.

EWE: Egblɔ nu si tae la na Nyɔ! talawo.
ENGLISH: He explained his reasons to Awake!

EWE: Míeɖe kuku ƒo nu tso ɖokuiwò ŋu na mí vie.
ENGLISH: Please tell us a little about your background.

EWE: Yan-Der Hsuuw
ENGLISH: Yan-Der Hsuuw

EWE: Wodzim le ƒe 1966 me eye menɔ Taiwan tsi.
ENGLISH: I was born in 1966 and grew up in Taiwan.

EWE: Tao subɔsubɔha kple Buddha subɔsubɔha mee dzinyelawo nɔ.
ENGLISH: My parents’ religion was based on both Taoism and Buddhism.

EWE: Togbɔ be míedea ta agu na tɔgbui kukuwo hedoa gbe ɖa na nɔnɔmewɔwɔwo hã la, míeka ɖe edzi be Wɔla aɖee wɔ nuwo o.
ENGLISH: Although we worshipped our ancestors and prayed to images, we never entertained the concept of a personal Creator.

EWE: Nu ka tae nèsrɔ̃ nu tso nu gbagbewo ŋu?
ENGLISH: Why did you study biology?

EWE: Esi menɔ ɖevime la, meléa be na aƒemelãwo, eye medina be masrɔ̃ ale si mawɔ akpe ɖe lãwo kple amegbetɔ siwo le fu kpem la ŋu.
ENGLISH: As a child, I liked caring for pets, and I wanted to learn how to relieve animals and people of suffering.

EWE: Eya ta mesrɔ̃ nu tso ale si mawɔ atike na lãwo woanɔ lãmesẽ me ŋu vie, eye emegbe meva srɔ̃ nu tso fugboewo hã ŋu be wòakpe ɖe ŋunye mase ale si agbe wɔ dze egɔme la gɔme.
ENGLISH: For a time, I studied veterinary medicine, and later I studied embryology a field that I hoped would also shed light on the origin of life.

EWE: Ɣemaɣi la, èxɔ amedzɔtsolãme dzi se.
ENGLISH: You believed in evolution at the time.

EWE: Àte ŋu agblɔ nu si tae?
ENGLISH: Can you tell us why?

EWE: Yunivɛsiti nufialagãwo fia nu be amegbetɔ dzɔ tso lã me, eye wogblɔ be kpeɖodzi le eŋu.
ENGLISH: The university professors taught evolution, claiming that evidence supports it.

EWE: Mexɔ woƒe nya sia dzi se.
ENGLISH: I believed them.

EWE: Nu kae na nèva dze Biblia xexlẽ gɔme?
ENGLISH: Why did you start reading the Bible?

EWE: Taɖodzinu eve ye nɔ asinye.
ENGLISH: My motive was twofold.

EWE: Gbã la, mesusuna be le mawu gbogbo siwo amewo subɔna dome la, ɖeka aɖe anɔ anyi si kpɔ ŋusẽ wu bubuawo katã.
ENGLISH: First, I reasoned that of the many gods that people worship, one must be greater than the others.

EWE: Gake wo dometɔ kae?
ENGLISH: But which one?

EWE: Evelia, menya be Biblia nye agbalẽ si ŋu ame geɖe dea asixɔxɔe.
ENGLISH: Second, I knew that the Bible is a highly respected book.

EWE: Eya ta medze Biblia sɔsrɔ̃ ƒe kpekpewo dede gɔme.
ENGLISH: So I joined Bible study classes.

EWE: Esime menɔ nu srɔ̃m le Katolikotɔwo ƒe yunivɛsiti aɖe me le Leuven, Belgium le ƒe 1992 me la, meyi Katolikotɔwo ƒe sɔlemeha aɖe me ɖabia woƒe nunɔla be wòakpe ɖe ŋunye mase Biblia gɔme, gake egbe.
ENGLISH: When I started studying at Belgium’s Catholic University of Leuven in 1992, I visited a Catholic church and asked the priest to help me understand the Bible, but he declined my request.

EWE: Ke aleke nèwɔ kpɔ ŋuɖoɖo na wò Biblia me biabiawo?
ENGLISH: So how was your spiritual hunger satisfied?

Yes.

ENGLISH: Finally, I concluded that this Bible prophecy had come true on time

ENGLISH: The idea of a Creator was new to me, so I decided to do my own research on the subject

EWE: Nusɔsrɔ̃ tso Wɔla aɖe ŋu la nye nu yeye nam, ta meɖoe be nye ŋutɔ maku nu me tso nyaa ŋu.

EWE: Aʋawɔwɔ dziŋɔwo.​ Mateo 24:7; Nyaɖeɖefia 6:4.

"​ 2 Timoteo 3:1-4.

Yes.

ENGLISH: (Revelation 12:​7-​12) Satan’s influence on mankind can be seen in many of the bad attitudes and actions that make the last days "critical times hard to deal with. "​ 2 Timothy 3:1.

EWE: Susuŋutinunyala Aɖe Ƒe Xɔse
ENGLISH: A Brain Pathologist Explains His Faith

EWE: NUFIALAGÃ Rajesh Kalaria, si le Newcastle Yunivɛsiti le England la le nu srɔ̃m tso amegbetɔwo ƒe susu ŋu wu ƒe 40.
ENGLISH: PROFESSOR Rajesh Kalaria, of Newcastle University, England, has studied the human brain for more than 40 years.

EWE: Tsãa, exɔe se be ɖe nuwo dzɔ le wo ɖokui si.
ENGLISH: He used to believe in evolution.

EWE: Gake eva trɔ susu emegbe.
ENGLISH: But later, he changed his views.

EWE: Nyɔ! magazinea talawo bia gbee tso eƒe xɔse kpakple eƒe dɔa ŋu.
ENGLISH: Awake! asked him about his work and faith.

EWE: Míeɖe kuku subɔsubɔha ka mee nènɔ tsã?
ENGLISH: Please tell us about your religious background.

EWE: Wodzi tɔnye le India, eye togbɔ be Indiatɔe danye nye hã Uganda ye wodzii le.
ENGLISH: My father was born in India, and my mother, although of Indian origin, was born in Uganda.

EWE: Hindutɔwo ƒe dzixɔsewo koŋue kpɔ ŋusẽ ɖe wo dzi.
ENGLISH: Their lives were largely governed by Hindu customs.

EWE: Mí ame etɔ̃e wodzi eye nyee nye evelia.
ENGLISH: I am the second of three children.

EWE: Míenɔ Nairobi, le Kenya.
ENGLISH: We lived in Nairobi, Kenya.

EWE: Hindutɔ geɖewo hã nɔ afi ma.
ENGLISH: Many other Hindu people lived nearby.

EWE: Nu kae na dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunya va dzɔ dzi na wò?
ENGLISH: What stimulated your interest in science?

EWE: Lãwo ƒe nu dzɔa dzi nam eye zi geɖe la, nye kple xɔ̃nyewo míezɔa mɔ legbeewo ɖatsia avewo me be míakpɔ lãwo.
ENGLISH: I was always interested in animals, and I often went hiking and camping with my friends to see the spectacular wildlife.

EWE: Dɔ si koŋ medi be mawɔe nye be manye lãwo ƒe ɖɔkta.
ENGLISH: My initial goal was to be a veterinary surgeon.

EWE: Gake esi medo le asinudɔsrɔ̃suku aɖe le Nairobi la, meyi London Yunivɛsiti le England, va srɔ̃ nu tso ale si dɔlékuiwo wɔna tsina ŋu.
ENGLISH: But after graduating from a technical college in Nairobi, I went to England to study pathology at the University of London.

EWE: Emegbe meva srɔ̃ nu tso amegbetɔwo ƒe ahɔhɔ̃ koŋ ŋu.
ENGLISH: Later, I specialized in research into the human brain.

EWE: Ðe wò sukunusɔsrɔ̃wo kpɔ ŋusẽ ɖe wò dzixɔsewo dzia?
ENGLISH: Did your studies affect your religious beliefs?
Yes.

EWE: Esi menɔ nu geɖe srɔ̃m tso dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunya ŋu la, eva sesẽ nam be mayi edzi axɔ Hindutɔwo ƒe nyakpakpawo kple kɔnuwo dzi ase.
ENGLISH: The more I studied science, the harder I found it to believe in Hindu mythology and traditions, such as the worship of animals and images.

EWE: Esia ƒe ɖewoe nye lãwo kple legbawo subɔsubɔ.
ENGLISH: Why did you accept the teaching of evolution?

EWE: Esi menye ɖevi la, ame siwo dome menɔ la xɔe se be Afrika ye nɔnɔmetɔtrɔ dze egɔme tsoe, eye wofiaa nu siawo mí le suku enuenu.
ENGLISH: In my younger years, many people around me held the view that human evolution began in Africa, and we often discussed this idea at school.

EWE: Azɔ hã, nufialawo kple yunivɛsiti nufialagãwo na mí sukuviawo míexɔe se be dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyala gãwo katã ka ɖe edzi be ɖe nuwo dzɔ le wo ɖokui si.
ENGLISH: Also, the teachers and university professors gave us students the impression that all respected scientists believe in evolution.

EWE: Esi ɣeyiɣiawo va nɔ yiyim la, wò susu va trɔ le afi si agbe dzɔ tso ŋu.
ENGLISH: In time you reconsidered the question of the origin of life.

EWE: Nu ka tae?
ENGLISH: Why?

EWE: Menɔ nu srɔ̃m tso nu gbagbewo kple woƒe wɔwɔme ŋu ƒe aɖewo va se ɖe esime sukuhati aɖe va gblɔ nu siwo srɔ̃m wònɔ le Biblia me tso Yehowa Ðasefowo gbɔ la nam.
ENGLISH: I had been studying biology and anatomy for some years when a fellow student told me what he was learning about the Bible from Jehovah’s Witnesses.

EWE: Medi be manya nu geɖe.
ENGLISH: I became curious.

EWE: Eya ta esi Ðasefoawo va wɔ takpekpe aɖe le míaƒe sukua ƒe takpexɔ me le Nairobi la, nye hã mede.
ENGLISH: So when the Witnesses held an assembly at our college hall in Nairobi, I attended.

EWE: Emegbe Ðasefo eve siwo nye dutanyanyuigblɔlawo va ɖe Biblia me nufiafia aɖewo me nam.
ENGLISH: Later, two Witness missionaries explained some Bible teachings to me.

EWE: Esi mekpɔe be woxɔ Wɔla Gã aɖe dzi se eye be egbɔe míakpɔ agbemebiabia vevitɔwo ƒe ŋuɖoɖowo le la, nyemebui kura be nyakpakpa aɖee o.
ENGLISH: Their belief in a Grand Designer who has the answers to life’s big questions did not sound like mythology.

EWE: Enya se nam eye susu le eme hã.
ENGLISH: It appealed to me as being reasonable.

EWE: Ðe nu siwo nèsrɔ̃ tso ahɔhɔ̃a ŋu na wòsesẽ na wò be nàxɔe ase be ɖe wowɔ nuwoa?
ENGLISH: Did your medical knowledge hinder your belief in creation?

EWE: Kura o!
ENGLISH: On the contrary!

EWE: Esi menɔ nu srɔ̃m tso nuwo ƒe wɔwɔme ŋu la, meva kpɔe be wowɔ nu gbagbewo le mɔ wɔnuku aɖe ŋutɔ nu.
ENGLISH: As I studied anatomy, I saw how well-designed and complex living things are.

EWE: Be míagblɔ be naneke mefiaa mɔ nuwɔwɔ wɔnuku siawo o la nye nu si me susu megava nɔ nam o.
ENGLISH: To attribute such a high level of sophistication to an unguided process no longer made sense to me.

EWE: Àte ŋu agblɔ eƒe kpɔɖeŋu aɖe na mía?
ENGLISH: Can you give us an example?

EWE: Medze nusɔsrɔ̃ tso amegbetɔ ƒe ahɔhɔ̃ ŋu tso ƒe 1970-awo me, eye ahɔhɔ̃a ƒe dɔwɔwɔ gawɔa nuku nam kokoko.
ENGLISH: I have studied the human brain since the early 1970’s, and this remarkable organ never ceases to amaze me.

EWE: Ahɔhɔ̃a koŋ ye nana míebua tame, ɖoa ŋku nu dzi eye wònana míaƒe ŋutinu vovovoawo katã wɔa dɔ.
ENGLISH: It is the seat of thought and memory and the control center for many bodily functions.

EWE: Eya kee nana lãmesidzenu vovovoawo wɔa dɔ eye wòwɔa nyatakaka siwo tso ametia me kple esiwo tso ametia godo siaa ŋu dɔ.
ENGLISH: The brain is also the hub of our many senses, interpreting information that comes from both inside and outside the body.

EWE: Susu si ta míaƒe ahɔhɔ̃a wɔa dɔ nyuie nye be eme tsiwo kple ahɔhɔ̃menugbagbeviwo wɔa dɔ aduadu le mɔ wɔnuku aɖe nu.
ENGLISH: Our brain functions the way it does largely because of its complex chemistry and intricate networks of neurons, the primary brain cells.

EWE: Ahɔhɔ̃menugbagbevi biliɔn gbogbo aɖewoe le amegbetɔ ƒe ahɔhɔ̃ me, eye wowɔa dɔ aduadu kple wo nɔewo to lãmeka falɛfalɛ legbee siwo woyɔna le Eŋlisigbe me be axons dzi.
ENGLISH: The human brain has many billions of neurons, which communicate with one another through long fibers called axons.

EWE: Ahɔhɔ̃menugbagbevi siawo dometɔ ɖeka ate ŋu awɔ dɔ aduadu kple ahɔhɔ̃menugbagbevi bubuwo to lãmeka falɛfalɛ (dendrites) siwo dzea alɔ la dzi.
ENGLISH: From these, a single neuron may make many thousands of connections with other neurons by way of branching fibers called dendrites.

EWE: Esia wɔe be xexlẽme mele ale si ahɔhɔ̃mekawo de nu wo nɔewo me ŋu o!
ENGLISH: As a result, the total number of connections in the brain is astronomical!

EWE: Azɔ hã ahɔhɔ̃menugbagbevi akpeakpe siawo kple lãmeka falɛfalɛ siawo wɔa dɔ ɖe ɖoɖo nyui nu eye wometɔtɔna o.
ENGLISH: What is more, this dense forest of neurons and dendrites is, not chaotic, but precise.

EWE: Ale si "wolɔ̃ " ɖe wo nɔewo me la wɔ nuku ŋutɔ.
ENGLISH: It is an amazing feat of "wiring. "

EWE: Míeɖe kuku ɖe eme.
ENGLISH: Please explain.

EWE: Ahɔhɔ̃mekawo dzea dɔwɔwɔ ɖe ɖoɖo nu gɔme ne vidzĩwo le dɔ me kple ne wodzi wo vɔ megbe.
ENGLISH: The wiring progresses in a most orderly way during a baby’s development in the womb as well as postnatally.

EWE: Ahɔhɔ̃menugbagbeviwo ɖoa lãmeka falɛfalɛwo ɖa be woavae tsiã kple ahɔhɔ̃menugbagbevi bubu siwo dome didi tso wo gbɔ sentimeta ʋɛ aɖewo gake dometsotsoa adidi ŋutɔ ne lãmenugbagbeviwo gbɔe woɖo wo ɖo.
ENGLISH: Neurons send out fibers to target neurons that may be a few centimeters away​ a vast distance on the cellular level.

EWE: Gake menye lãmenugbagbevi aɖe koŋ koe lãmeka falɛfalɛa yina ɖatsiãna kple o ke eƒe akpa aɖe koŋ ye.
ENGLISH: The target of a fiber, by the way, may be not just a specific cell but a specific part of that cell.

EWE: Ne lãmeka falɛfalɛ yeye aɖe dze tso ahɔhɔ̃meka aɖe me la, lãmetsiwo fiaa mɔe eye wogblɔna nɛ be "tɔ, " "dzo " alo "trɔ " va se ɖe esime wòaɖo afi si yim wòle.
ENGLISH: As a new fiber branches out from a neuron, it is guided by chemical signposts that say such things as "stop, " "go, " or "turn " until the fiber reaches its target.

EWE: Ne womefia mɔ lãmeka falɛfalɛ siawo nyuie o la, woabu.
ENGLISH: Without clear instructions, growing fibers would soon get lost.

EWE: Ale si nu siawo katã wɔa dɔ nukutɔe la nɔ te ɖe mɔfiame siwo woŋlɔ ɖe domenyiŋusẽfianua (DNA, ADN) me la dzi.
ENGLISH: The whole process is brilliantly orchestrated, starting with the instructions written in our DNA.

EWE: Togbɔ be míenya nu siawo hã la, nu gbogbo aɖewo gali siwo mímenya tso ale si ahɔhɔ̃a wɔa dɔe, ale si wòwɔna ɖoa ŋku nu dzi, ɖea seselelãmewo fiana kple ale si wòbua nuwo ŋu la nyuie o.
ENGLISH: That said, we are far from understanding fully how the brain develops and functions, including how it forms memories, emotions, and thoughts.

EWE: Le gonyeme la, ale si ahɔhɔ̃a wɔa dɔe ɖeɖe dzaa fiam be ame aɖe si ƒe susu de ŋgɔ sãsãsã wu mía tɔ la li, eye mehiã be maƒo nu tso ale si ahɔhɔ̃a wɔa dɔe tsitotsito gɔ̃ hã ŋu o.
ENGLISH: For me, just the fact that the brain works​ not to mention how well it works and how beautifully it develops ​points to a mind far superior to our own.

EWE: Nu kae na nèva zu Yehowa Ðasefo?
ENGLISH: Why did you become one of Jehovah’s Witnesses?

EWE: Ðasefoawo na mekpɔ kpeɖodziwo be Biblia nye Mawu ƒe Nya.
ENGLISH: The Witnesses showed me evidence that the Bible is God’s Word.

EWE: Le kpɔɖeŋu me, menye dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyagbalẽe Biblia nye o, gake ne ele nu ƒom tso dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunya ŋu la edena pɛpɛpɛ.
ENGLISH: For example, the Bible is not a science book, but when it touches on scientific matters, it is consistently correct.

EWE: Nyagblɔɖi siwo de pɛpɛpɛ hã le eme.
ENGLISH: It also contains accurate prophecies.

EWE: Eye ame siwo wɔna ɖe emenyawo dzi la nɔa agbe nyui.
ENGLISH: And it improves the lives of those who apply its teachings.

EWE: Ale si mele agbe nɔm fifia la hã nye kpeɖodzi ɖeka.
ENGLISH: My own life is evidence of that.

EWE: Tso esime meva zu Yehowa Ðasefo le ƒe 1973 me la, Bibliae nye agbalẽ vevitɔ si fiaa mɔm.
ENGLISH: Since I became one of Jehovah’s Witnesses in 1973, the Bible has been my guidebook.

EWE: Esia wɔe be nye dzi dze eme eye taɖodzinu va le nye agbe ŋu.
ENGLISH: As a result, my life has become truly satisfying and purposeful.

ENGLISH: He once believed in evolution, but after becoming a research scientist, he changed his mind.

EWE: Egblɔ nu si tae la na Nyɔ! talawo.
ENGLISH: He explained his reasons to Awake!

EWE: Míeɖe kuku ƒo nu tso ɖokuiwò ŋu na mí vie.
ENGLISH: Please tell us a little about your background.

EWE: Yan-Der Hsuuw
ENGLISH: Yan-Der Hsuuw

EWE: Wodzim le ƒe 1966 me eye menɔ Taiwan tsi.
ENGLISH: I was born in 1966 and grew up in Taiwan.

EWE: Tao subɔsubɔha kple Buddha subɔsubɔha mee dzinyelawo nɔ.
ENGLISH: My parents’ religion was based on both Taoism and Buddhism.

EWE: Togbɔ be míedea ta agu na tɔgbui kukuwo hedoa gbe ɖa na nɔnɔmewɔwɔwo hã la, míeka ɖe edzi be Wɔla aɖee wɔ nuwo o.
ENGLISH: Although we worshipped our ancestors and prayed to images, we never entertained the concept of a personal Creator.

EWE: Nu ka tae nèsrɔ̃ nu tso nu gbagbewo ŋu?
ENGLISH: Why did you study biology?

EWE: Esi menɔ ɖevime la, meléa be na aƒemelãwo, eye medina be masrɔ̃ ale si mawɔ akpe ɖe lãwo kple amegbetɔ siwo le fu kpem la ŋu.
ENGLISH: As a child, I liked caring for pets, and I wanted to learn how to relieve animals and people of suffering.

EWE: Eya ta mesrɔ̃ nu tso ale si mawɔ atike na lãwo woanɔ lãmesẽ me ŋu vie, eye emegbe meva srɔ̃ nu tso fugboewo hã ŋu be wòakpe ɖe ŋunye mase ale si agbe wɔ dze egɔme la gɔme.
ENGLISH: For a time, I studied veterinary medicine, and later I studied embryology a field that I hoped would also shed light on the origin of life.

EWE: Ɣemaɣi la, èxɔ amedzɔtsolãme dzi se.
ENGLISH: You believed in evolution at the time.

EWE: Àte ŋu agblɔ nu si tae?
ENGLISH: Can you tell us why?

EWE: Yunivɛsiti nufialagãwo fia nu be amegbetɔ dzɔ tso lã me, eye wogblɔ be kpeɖodzi le eŋu.
ENGLISH: The university professors taught evolution, claiming that evidence supports it.

EWE: Mexɔ woƒe nya sia dzi se.
ENGLISH: I believed them.

EWE: Nu kae na nèva dze Biblia xexlẽ gɔme?
ENGLISH: Why did you start reading the Bible?

EWE: Taɖodzinu eve ye nɔ asinye.
ENGLISH: My motive was twofold.

EWE: Gbã la, mesusuna be le mawu gbogbo siwo amewo subɔna dome la, ɖeka aɖe anɔ anyi si kpɔ ŋusẽ wu bubuawo katã.
ENGLISH: First, I reasoned that of the many gods that people worship, one must be greater than the others.

EWE: Gake wo dometɔ kae?
ENGLISH: But which one?

EWE: Evelia, menya be Biblia nye agbalẽ si ŋu ame geɖe dea asixɔxɔe.
ENGLISH: Second, I knew that the Bible is a highly respected book.

EWE: Eya ta medze Biblia sɔsrɔ̃ ƒe kpekpewo dede gɔme.
ENGLISH: So I joined Bible study classes.

EWE: Esime menɔ nu srɔ̃m le Katolikotɔwo ƒe yunivɛsiti aɖe me le Leuven, Belgium le ƒe 1992 me la, meyi Katolikotɔwo ƒe sɔlemeha aɖe me ɖabia woƒe nunɔla be wòakpe ɖe ŋunye mase Biblia gɔme, gake egbe.
ENGLISH: When I started studying at Belgium’s Catholic University of Leuven in 1992, I visited a Catholic church and asked the priest to help me understand the Bible, but he declined my request.

EWE: Ke aleke nèwɔ kpɔ ŋuɖoɖo na wò Biblia me biabiawo?
ENGLISH: So how was your spiritual hunger satisfied?

EWE: Le ƒe eve megbe, esime mekpɔtɔ nɔ Belgium nɔ nu srɔ̃m la, medo go Yehowa Ðasefo aɖe si ŋkɔe nye Ruth tso Poland.
ENGLISH: Two years later, while I was still in Belgium doing scientific research, I met a Polish lady named Ruth, who was one of Jehovah’s Witnesses.

EWE: Esrɔ̃ Chinagbe be wòate ŋu akpe ɖe yunivɛsitivi siwo di be yewoasrɔ̃ nu tso Mawu ŋu la ŋu.
ENGLISH: She had learned Chinese in order to help university students who wanted to learn about God.

EWE: Medo gbe ɖa be makpɔ ame aɖe wòakpe ɖe ŋunye nenema, eya ta dzi dzɔm esi medo goe.
ENGLISH: I had prayed for such help, so I was delighted to meet her.

EWE: Ruth fiam be togbɔ be Biblia menye dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyagbalẽ o hã, emenyawo wɔ ɖeka kple dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunya.
ENGLISH: Ruth showed me that the Bible, while not a science book, is in harmony with science.

EWE: Le kpɔɖeŋu me, Biblia ŋlɔla David gblɔ na Mawu le gbedodoɖa me be: "Wò ŋkuwo kpɔm esime menye ʋukɔe; eye woŋlɔ eŋu nuwo katã ɖe wò agbalẽ me, le ŋkeke siwo me wowɔ wo, esime wo dometɔ aɖeke medo haɖe o. "
ENGLISH: For example, the Bible writer David said in prayer to God: "Your eyes even saw me as an embryo; all its parts were written in your book regarding the days when they were formed, before any of them existed. "

EWE: (Psalmo 139:16) Togbɔ be hakpanya mee David gblɔ nya sia le hã la, ne míagblɔe la, nyateƒee wòto!
ENGLISH: (Psalm 139:16) Although David was using poetic language, in principle, he was right!

EWE: Hafi míaƒe ŋutinuwo nado la, mɔfiame siwo dzi woazɔ ɖo la li xoxo.
ENGLISH: Even before body parts form, the instructions for their development are all there.

EWE: Ale si Biblia me nyawo de pɛpɛpɛ la na meka ɖe edzi be Mawu ƒe Nyae wònye.
ENGLISH: The accuracy of the Bible helped convince me that it is God’s Word.

EWE: Meva se egɔme hã be Mawu vavã ɖeka, si nye Yehowa koe li.
ENGLISH: I also began to appreciate that there is only one true God, Jehovah.

EWE: Nu kae na nèva ka ɖe edzi be Mawu gbɔe agbe dzɔ tso?
ENGLISH: What convinced you that God created life?

EWE: Taɖodzinu si le numekuku si dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyalawo wɔna ŋue nye be woake ɖe nyateƒea ŋu, ke menye be woada asi ɖe susu siwo le amewo si dzi o.
ENGLISH: A goal of scientific research is to find the truth, not to support preconceived ideas.

EWE: Esi meva nɔ nu srɔ̃m tso ale si fugboe wɔna tsina ŋu la, metrɔ susu, eye meƒo nya ta be Wɔla lae wɔ nuwo.
ENGLISH: My study of embryo development led me to change my view that is, I concluded that life was created.

EWE: Le kpɔɖeŋu me, ne mɔ̃ɖaŋudɔwɔlawo le mɔ̃ aɖe wɔm la, wokpɔa egbɔ be wode eƒe akpa ɖe sia ɖe teƒe si wòle be wòanɔ la pɛpɛpɛ.
ENGLISH: To illustrate, engineers design assembly lines so that the right parts are fitted together in the right order and in the right way.

EWE: Nenemae fugboe hã le, gake ale si fugboe ya wɔna tsina gɔme sese sesẽ ale gbegbe.
ENGLISH: Embryo development is somewhat similar but vastly more complex.

EWE: Nu bliboa dzea egɔme ne ŋutsu ƒe tsi kple nyɔnu ƒe azi do go, alo menye nenemae oa?
ENGLISH: The process all starts with a single fertilized cell, doesn’t it?
Yes.

EWE: Lãmenugbagbevi sue ma si ŋku mate ŋu akpɔ o la mana, eye wòyia edzi nɔa mamam.
ENGLISH: That microscopic cell then divides, starting the process of cell division.

EWE: Lãmenugbagbeviawo ƒe agbɔsɔsɔ dzina ɖe edzi teƒe eve tso gaƒoƒo 12 va se ɖe 24 hena ɣeyiɣi aɖe.
ENGLISH: For a time, the number of cells doubles every 12 to 24 hours.

EWE: Le ɣeyiɣi sia me la, lãmenugbagbevi aɖe dona.
ENGLISH: Early in this process, cells called stem cells form.

ENGLISH: My study of embryo development led me to conclude that life was created

EWE: Gbã la, wonyea ʋukɔe siwo me lãmenuwo kple ŋutinuwo va dona tso.
ENGLISH: First they assemble into tissues that will in turn assemble themselves into organs and limbs.

EWE: Mɔ̃ɖaŋudɔwɔla kae aku drɔ̃e be yeate ŋu aŋlɔ mɔfiame siwo dzi fugboe ato atsi la ɖi?
ENGLISH: What engineer even dreams of writing instructions for such a process?

EWE: Ke hã, woŋlɔ mɔfiame si dzi fugboe ato atsi la ɖe eƒe DNA me nukutɔe.
ENGLISH: Yet, the instructions for embryo development are superbly written in DNA.

EWE: Ne mede ŋugble tso ale si gbegbe esia wɔ nukui ŋu la, enana mekana ɖe edzi be Mawue wɔ nuwo.
ENGLISH: When I consider the beauty of it all, I’m convinced that life was designed by God.

EWE: Nu ka tae nèva zu Yehowa Ðasefo?
ENGLISH: Why did you become one of Jehovah’s Witnesses?

EWE: Kpuie ko la, lɔlɔ̃ si le wo dome ye.
ENGLISH: In a word, love.

EWE: Yesu Kristo gblɔ be: "Esia me amewo katã anyae le be nye nusrɔ̃lawo mienye, ne lɔlɔ̃ le mia dome. "
ENGLISH: Jesus Christ said: "By this all will know that you are my disciples if you have love among yourselves. "

EWE: (Yohanes 13:35) Ameŋkumemakpɔmakpɔ aɖeke mele lɔlɔ̃ sia me o.
ENGLISH: (John 13:35) That love is impartial.

EWE: Teƒe si ame aɖe tso, dekɔnu alo ŋutigbalẽ ƒe amadede mekpɔa ŋusẽ ɖe lɔlɔ̃ sia ɖeɖe fia dzi o.
ENGLISH: It is not influenced by a person’s nationality, culture, or skin color.

EWE: Esi medze hadede kple Ðasefowo la mekpɔ lɔlɔ̃ sia le wo dome eye woɖe lɔlɔ̃ sia fiam.
ENGLISH: I both observed and experienced that kind of love when I began to associate with the Witnesses.

ENGLISH: Dr. Céline Granolleras is a medical doctor in France who specializes in kidney disease.

ENGLISH: More than 20 years after becoming a doctor, she came to the conclusion that there is a Creator who cares for us.

ENGLISH: Awake! asked her about her work and her faith.

EWE: Ne ame aɖe biam be, ne Mawu meli o la, ke aleke agbe wɔ dze egɔme mahã la, meɖoa eŋu nɛ be: "Fifia dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyalawo mete ŋu ɖe eme haɖe o, gake gbe ɖeka woava kpɔ ŋuɖoɖo na nya ma. "
ENGLISH: If anyone asked me how life began if there is no God, I replied, "For now, scientists cannot explain it, but one day they will. "

ENGLISH: What made you study kidney disease?

ENGLISH: I studied at a medical school in Montpellier, France.

EWE: Nufialagã aɖe si le sukua me la ɖo aɖaŋu nam be masrɔ̃ nu tso ayikudɔ ŋu.
ENGLISH: A professor there spoke to me about working in nephrology, a branch of medicine involving the kidneys.

EWE: Dɔ sia bia numekuku kple dɔnɔwo gbɔ kpɔkpɔ le ɣeyiɣi ma ke me.
ENGLISH: The work combined research with the care of patients.

EWE: Dɔ sia tututu dim mele be mawɔ.
ENGLISH: That was just what I wanted.

ENGLISH: In 1990, I began taking part in research on the clinical use of recombinant erythropoietin (EPO) to control the production of red blood cells in our bones.

EWE: Ɣemaɣi la, wobunɛ be enye numekuku yeye.
ENGLISH: At that time, it was considered a relatively new field of research.

EWE: Nu kae na nèva di be yeanya ne Mawu li?
ENGLISH: What made you start thinking about God?

EWE: Tso keke ƒe 1979 me la, Yehowa Ðasefowo va nɔ Biblia srɔ̃m kple srɔ̃nye Floréal.
ENGLISH: Back in 1979, my husband, Floréal, started studying the Bible with Jehovah’s Witnesses.

EWE: Gake nyemetsɔ ɖeke le eme o.
ENGLISH: But I was not interested.

EWE: Esi menɔ ɖevime la, mawusubɔsubɔ ti kɔ nam.
ENGLISH: As a child, I had had enough of religion.

EWE: Ke hã srɔ̃nye kple mía viwo va zu Yehowa Ðasefowo, eye medidi o mía xɔlɔ̃wo katã kloe zu Yehowa Ðasefowo.
ENGLISH: Nevertheless, my husband and children became Witnesses, and soon nearly all our friends were Witnesses.

EWE: Mía xɔlɔ̃awo dometɔ ɖeka si ŋkɔe nye Patricia ɖo aɖaŋu nam be manɔ gbe dom ɖa.
ENGLISH: One of them, Patricia, suggested that I try praying.

ENGLISH: Years later, I started to wonder about the meaning of life, and I remembered Patricia’s words.

ENGLISH: I began to pray for understanding.

EWE: Nu ka tae nèva di be yeanya tameɖoɖo si le agbea ŋu?
ENGLISH: What made you wonder about the meaning of life?

EWE: Esi ŋɔdzinuwɔlawo dze Xexeame Katã ƒe Asitsaƒegã si le New York dzi la, mebia ɖokuinye be nu ka tae nu vɔ̃ɖi wɔwɔ xɔ aƒe ɖe amegbetɔwo dome mahã.
ENGLISH: The terrorist attack on the World Trade Center in New York made me wonder why there is so much evil in society.

ENGLISH: I thought: ‘Religious extremism endangers our future.

ENGLISH: Yet here I am surrounded by Jehovah’s Witnesses who are peaceful.

EWE: Woawo ya to vovo sãsãsã na zazɛ̃nyahelawo.
ENGLISH: They are not extremists.

EWE: Wowɔna ɖe Biblia me nyawo dzi.
ENGLISH: They follow the Bible.

EWE: Ðewohĩ ahiã be nye hã madzro Biblia me kpɔ.’
ENGLISH: Perhaps I should look into what it says.’

EWE: Ale wɔ mede asi Biblia xexlẽ me.
ENGLISH: So I began reading the Bible for myself.

EWE: Ðe wòsesẽ na wò be nàxɔe ase be Wɔla aɖe li le esi nènye ɖɔkta ta?
ENGLISH: As a doctor, did you find it difficult to believe in a Creator?

EWE: Ao.
ENGLISH: No.

EWE: Mekpɔa ŋudzedze ɖe ale si míaƒe ametia ƒe wɔwɔme wɔ nukue la ŋu ŋutɔ.
ENGLISH: I had a deep respect for our body’s sophisticated design.

EWE: Le kpɔɖeŋu me, ale si míaƒe ayiku nana be ʋumenugbagbevi dzĩwo ƒe agbɔsɔsɔ dana sɔna le míaƒe ʋu me la wɔ nuku nam ŋutɔ.
ENGLISH: For example, the way our kidneys control the amount of red cells in our blood is awe-inspiring.

ENGLISH: Why do you say that?

EWE: Meva nyɔ le ɖokuinye me be Mawu koe ate ŋu awɔ nu wɔnuku mawo gbegbe
ENGLISH: It struck me that only God could design such an elegant system

ENGLISH: As you may know, red blood cells transport oxygen.

EWE: Ne ʋu sɔgbɔ do le ŋuwò alo nèle teƒe kɔkɔ aɖe la, ɔksidzin masɔ gbɔ le lã me na wò o.
ENGLISH: If you lose a lot of blood or if you go to a high altitude, your body will lack oxygen.

EWE: Míaƒe ayikuwo dea dzesi ɔksidzin ƒe agbɔsɔsɔ si le lã me na mí.
ENGLISH: Our kidneys have oxygen sensors.

EWE: Ne wode dzesii be ɔksidzin mesɔ gbɔ le lã me na mí kura o la, wonana be lãmetsi si nana be ʋumenugbagbevi dzĩwo dzina ɖe edzi la sɔna gbɔ ɖe edzi abe teƒe akpe ɖeka ene.
ENGLISH: When they detect an oxygen shortage in the blood, they activate the production of EPO, and the level of EPO in the blood may rise as much as a thousandfold.

EWE: Lãmetsi sia nana be ƒutomemiwo wɔa ʋumenugbagbevi dzĩ yeyewo, eye ʋumenugbagbevi siawo tsɔa ɔksidzin gbogbo aɖewo yia ŋutilã ƒe akpa vovovowo.
ENGLISH: The EPO stimulates the bone marrow to produce more red cells, which in turn transport more oxygen.

EWE: Ewɔ nuku loo!
ENGLISH: It’s wonderful!

EWE: Togbɔ be mesrɔ̃ nu siawo hã la, ƒe ewo megbe hafi meva nyɔ le ɖokuinye me be Mawu koe ate ŋu awɔ nu wɔnuku mawo gbegbe.
ENGLISH: Strangely, I studied this process for ten years before it struck me that only God could design such an elegant system.

ENGLISH: What was your impression of the Bible?

ENGLISH: Its advice is so practical that it must come from a source higher than man.

ENGLISH: Jesus’ character fascinated me.

EWE: Mekpɔe be ame ŋutɔŋutɔe wònye.
ENGLISH: I saw that he was a real person.

ENGLISH: He had feelings, and he had friends.

ENGLISH: Since I didn’t want to use the publications of Jehovah’s Witnesses, I did research in encyclopedias and other reference works when questions arose.

EWE: Nu kawo ŋue nèkua nu me le?
ENGLISH: What did you research?

EWE: Meku nu me le ŋutinyagbalẽwo me . . .
ENGLISH: I researched history books . . .

EWE: Mlɔeba meƒo nya ta be Biblia ƒe nyagblɔɖi sia va eme ɖe ɣeyiɣi dzi pɛpɛpɛ
ENGLISH: Finally, I concluded that this Bible prophecy had come true on time

ENGLISH: Among other things, I was intrigued by the way the Bible foretold the year of Jesus’ baptism.

ENGLISH: It shows exactly how much time would elapse between the 20th year of the reign of the Persian ruler Artaxerxes and the year Jesus would present himself as the Messiah.
