EWE: Wolɔ̃a nuto ma yɔyɔ be mɔlu kple tɔmelã ƒe anyigba elabe nuɖuɖu bɔ ɖe afi ma ale gbegbe.
ENGLISH: It is a subtropical area famous for its food production, so it is often called the land of rice and fish.

EWE: Esi menye ɖevi la, mebiaa ɖokuinye be: ‘Nu ka tae nuɖuɖu viviwo bɔ ɖe xexea me alea?
ENGLISH: As a child, I used to wonder: ‘Why does nature provide so many tasty foods?

EWE: Ðe wodzɔ le wo ɖokui sia?
ENGLISH: Did they come about by chance?

EWE: Wo dometɔ kae dzɔ gbã, koklovi alo koklozi?’
ENGLISH: Which came first the chicken or the egg?’

EWE: Mawudzimaxɔselawo bɔ ɖe China, eya ta wofiam le suku be ɖeko nu gbagbewo dzɔ le wo ɖokui si.
ENGLISH: Atheism is predominant in China, so at school I was taught about evolution.

EWE: Ƒo nu tso wò ƒometɔwo hã ŋu na mí.
ENGLISH: What about your family?

EWE: Dzinyelawo mexɔ Mawu dzi se o.
ENGLISH: My parents were atheists.

EWE: Danye nye agbledela. Fofonye nye xɔtuɖaŋunyala eye wòɖo xɔtudɔwɔƒe aɖe.
ENGLISH: My mother did farmwork, while my father worked as an architect and established a construction company.

EWE: Nyee nye woƒe ŋutsuvi atɔ̃awo ƒe tsitsitɔ.
ENGLISH: I’m the eldest of their five sons.

EWE: Nublanuitɔe la, nɔvinye ŋutsu eve ku le woƒe ɖevime.
ENGLISH: Sadly, two of my brothers died young.

EWE: Esia na mexaa nu vevie eye mebia ɖokuinye be: ‘Nu ka tae ame kuna?
ENGLISH: That caused me much grief, and I wondered: ‘Why do people die?

EWE: Ðe magakpɔ nɔvinyeawo gbe ɖeka?’
ENGLISH: Will I ever see my brothers again?’

EWE: Nu ka tae nèsrɔ̃ dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunya?
ENGLISH: Why did you study science?

EWE: Nu si tae nye be mebua tame vevie tso dzɔdzɔmenuwo ŋu eye mesusui be nusɔsrɔ̃ ƒomevi sia akpe ɖe ŋunye makpɔ ŋuɖoɖo na nyabiase siwo ɖea fu nam tso ɖevime ke.
ENGLISH: I wanted to study physics because I was intrigued by the natural world and I thought physics might answer the questions that had intrigued me since childhood.

EWE: Nu kawo ŋue nèkua nu me le?
ENGLISH: What is your field of research?

EWE: Mesrɔ̃ nu tso ale si mana atɔm-menuwo ƒe dusisi nadzi ɖe edzi agogo kekeli ƒe dusisi.
ENGLISH: I explore ways of accelerating charged particles to speeds close to the speed of light.

EWE: Esia wɔe be mesrɔ̃ nu tso atɔm ƒe wɔwɔme ŋu.
ENGLISH: I do this to study the structure of atoms.

EWE: Meku nu me hã tso ale si woatrɔ asi le keklẽŋusẽ ƒe sesẽme ŋu wòato keklẽŋusẽ siwo woyɔna be microwave (micro-onde) ƒe sesẽme ŋu evɔ made keklẽŋusẽ si woyɔna be infrared (infrarouge) ƒe sesẽme nu o.
ENGLISH: I also investigate how to generate high-power radiation with a frequency between that of microwave and infrared radiation.

EWE: Togbɔ be ga tae mewɔa esia ɖo hã la, nu bubu si hã tae mewɔnɛ ɖoe nye be manya nu tso ale si xexea wɔ va dzɔ ŋu.
ENGLISH: Although my research has commercial value, it is also linked to efforts to understand how the universe began.

EWE: Aleke wòdzɔe be nèva tsɔ ɖe le Biblia me?
ENGLISH: How did you become interested in the Bible?

EWE: Le ƒe 1998 me la, Yehowa Ðasefo eve va gbɔnye le aƒe me.
ENGLISH: In 1998, two of Jehovah’s Witnesses visited my home.

EWE: Wogblɔ be yewoakpe ɖe ŋunye makpɔ ŋuɖoɖo na nye nyabiaseawo le Biblia me.
ENGLISH: They offered to show me the Bible’s answers to my questions.

EWE: Srɔ̃nye Huabi, si hã nye dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyala va wɔ ɖeka kpli mí le numedzodzroa me.
ENGLISH: My wife, Huabi, who is also a research scientist, joined us.

EWE: Togbɔ be zi gbãtɔe nye ema míekpɔ Biblia hã la, aɖaŋuɖoɖo nyui siwo le eme la wɔ dɔ ɖe mía dzi ŋutɔ.
ENGLISH: We had never seen a Bible before, but we were impressed by its practical advice.

EWE: Míekpɔ ale si Biblia ƒe aɖaŋuɖoɖowo dzi wɔwɔ ɖe vi na atsu kple asi siwo va dzroa nuwo me kpli mí.
ENGLISH: We noticed how the Witness couple who visited us benefited by applying Bible principles.

EWE: Dzi dzɔa wo eye wometsɔ nu geɖe do agba na wo ɖokui le agbe me o.
ENGLISH: They were happy and enjoyed an uncomplicated way of life.

EWE: Gake nu si Biblia gblɔ tso Mawu ŋu la na nye susu va nɔ wɔwɔm eveve be ɖe woanya wɔ xexea mahã.
ENGLISH: But what the Bible says about God set me to wondering again whether the universe could have been created.

EWE: Abe dzɔdzɔmeŋusẽŋununyala ene la, nye dɔe nye be mase dzɔdzɔmenuwo gɔme.
ENGLISH: As a physicist, my job is to understand nature.

EWE: Eya ta medi be magaku nuwo me tsitotsito.
ENGLISH: So I decided to give the facts some careful thought.

EWE: Abe dzɔdzɔmeŋusẽŋununyala ene la, nye dɔe nye be mase dzɔdzɔmenuwo gɔme.
ENGLISH: As a physicist, my job is to understand nature.

EWE: Eya ta medi be magaku nuwo me tsitotsito
ENGLISH: So I decided to give the facts some careful thought

EWE: Ke nu kawo ŋue nèva ke ɖo?
ENGLISH: What facts did you consider?

EWE: Gbã la, menya be nu vovovo siwo le ƒuƒoƒo me mate ŋu anɔ ɖoɖo nu o negbe ɖe nu bubu aɖe kpɔ ŋusẽ ɖe wo dzi.
ENGLISH: First, I knew that a closed system cannot become more organized or remain organized unless acted upon by an external agent.

EWE: Emae woyɔna be dzɔdzɔmeŋusẽ ƒe se evelia.
ENGLISH: That is the second law of thermodynamics.

EWE: Esi wònye be ɖe xexe gbahooa kple nu gbagbewo le ɖoɖo manyagblɔ aɖe nu ta la, meƒo nya ta be ame aɖee wɔ wo, eyae anye Wɔla la.
ENGLISH: Since the universe and life on earth are highly ordered, I concluded that they must be products of an external agent, a Creator.

EWE: Eveliae nye be edze abe ɖe wowɔ xexe gbahoo sia kple anyigba ale be agbe nanya nɔ le edzi ene.
ENGLISH: The second fact was that the universe and the earth seem to be specifically designed to support life.

EWE: Nu kae ɖo kpe edzi na wo be ɖe wowɔ nu gbagbewo?
ENGLISH: What evidence of design did you see?

EWE: Le nyateƒe me la, nu gbagbe siwo katã le anyigba dzi la hiã ɣe ƒe ŋusẽ hafi woate ŋu anɔ agbe.
ENGLISH: Practically all life on earth depends on energy from the sun.

EWE: Ne ŋusẽ sia tso ɣea gbɔ gbɔna anyigba la ezua keklẽŋusẽ le yame.
ENGLISH: This energy travels through space as radiation.

EWE: Keklẽŋusẽ sia va ɖoa anyigba hezua keklẽŋusẽ ƒomevi vovovowo.
ENGLISH: It comes to earth in a vast spectrum of wavelengths.

EWE: Woyɔa keklẽŋusẽ si ƒua du wu la be gamma ray (rayon gamma) si gblẽa ŋu.
ENGLISH: The shortest are the lethal gamma rays.

EWE: Esiwo kplɔe ɖoe nye X-ray (rayon X), ultraviolet ray, kekeli, infrared, microwave kple esi meɖoa anyigba kaba o, si nye radio ƒe gbeɖiɖixɔŋusẽwo.
ENGLISH: Then come X-rays, ultraviolet rays, visible light, infrared, microwaves, and the longest of all, radio waves.

EWE: Eɖe dzesi ŋutɔ be wowɔ ya si ƒo xlã míaƒe anyigba be wòaxe mɔ na keklẽŋusẽ siwo gblẽa nu evɔ wòaɖe mɔ na keklẽŋusẽ siwo ɖea vi na mí ya be woaɖo anyigba dzi.
ENGLISH: Remarkably, our atmosphere blocks much harmful radiation while allowing other needed radiation to reach the earth’s surface.

EWE: Nu ka tae nu ma wɔ dɔ ɖe dziwò nenema gbegbe?
ENGLISH: Why did that fact impress you?

EWE: Nya siwo wogblɔ ku ɖe nuwɔwɔwo ŋu le Biblia ƒe gɔmedzedze tso kekeli ŋu la wɔ dɔ ɖe dzinye ŋutɔ.
ENGLISH: I was intrigued by the introduction to the Bible’s creation account and its reference to light.

EWE: Afi ma gblɔ be: "Mawu gblɔ be: Kekeli nedo!
ENGLISH: It states: "God said: ‘Let there be light.’

EWE: Eye kekeli do. "
ENGLISH: Then there was light. "

EWE: Ɣe ƒe keklẽ si le xexe gbahooa me ƒe akpa sue aɖe koe amegbetɔwo tea ŋu kpɔna, ke hã kekeli hiã hafi nu gbagbewo nate ŋu anɔ nyigba dzi.
ENGLISH: Only a very narrow band of the vast spectrum of solar radiation is visible light, but light is vital for life.

EWE: Atiwo hiã na kekeli be woatsɔ awɔ woƒe nuɖuɖuwo, eye mí amegbetɔwo hã míehiã nɛ be míate ŋu akpɔ nu.
ENGLISH: Plants need it to produce food, and we need light to see.

EWE: Ale si kekeli wɔna tea ŋu va ɖoa anyigba dzi la mate ŋu anye nudogoɖenunu o.
ENGLISH: The atmosphere’s special transparency to light cannot be a coincidence.

EWE: Esi gawɔ nuku wue nye ale si ya si ƒo xlã anyigba ɖea mɔ ultraviolet-keklẽŋusẽ ʋɛ aɖe ko va ɖoa anyigba dzi.
ENGLISH: Even more remarkable is the tiny amount of ultraviolet light that reaches the earth’s surface. Why is that significant?

EWE: Nu kae ɖe dzesi le keklẽŋusẽ sia ŋu?
ENGLISH: Some ultraviolet radiation is critical.

EWE: Míehiã ultraviolet-keklẽŋusẽ ʋɛ aɖe be wòana nunyiame si woyɔna be vitamin D la míaƒe ŋutigbalẽ, enaa ŋusẽ nɔa míaƒe ƒuwo ŋu eye wòkpɔa mía ta tso kansa kple dɔléle bubuwo si me.
ENGLISH: We need a small amount of it on our skin to produce vitamin D, which is vital for bone health and evidently for protection from cancer and other diseases.

EWE: Gake ne keklẽŋusẽ sia sɔ gbɔ akpa la, enaa ŋutigbalẽmekansa kple ŋkudɔ mí.
ENGLISH: However, too much of this particular radiation causes skin cancer and eye cataracts.

EWE: Ne ya si ƒo xlã anyigba ɖe mɔ ɖe keklẽ sia ƒe sue aɖe si sɔ ŋu wòva ɖo anyigba dzi la, esɔna na mí ŋutɔ.
ENGLISH: In its natural state, the atmosphere allows only a tiny amount of this ultraviolet radiation to reach the earth’s surface and it is just the right amount.

EWE: Le nye ya gonyeme la, esia ɖo kpe edzi be ame aɖee wɔ anyigba kple nu gbagbewo.
ENGLISH: For me, that is evidence that someone designed the earth to sustain life.

EWE: Ʋɛʋɛʋɛ la, nye kple srɔ̃nye Huabi míeva ka ɖe edzi be Wɔla aɖe li eye be eyae na woŋlɔ Biblia.
ENGLISH: Gradually Huabi and I became convinced that there is a Creator and that he inspired the Bible.

EWE: Le ƒe 2005 me la, míezu Yehowa Ðasefowo eye míekpɔa gome le Biblia me gbedeasia fiafia amewo me.
ENGLISH: In 2005, we became Jehovah’s Witnesses, and now we share in teaching the Bible to others.

EWE: Atikeŋutinumekula Aɖe Ƒe Xɔse
ENGLISH: I Am Convinced That There Is a Creator "

EWE: Frédéric Dumoulin
ENGLISH: Frédéric Dumoulin

EWE: Frédéric Dumoulin ku nu me tso atikewɔwɔ ŋu le Ghent Yunivɛsiti si le Belgium ƒe ewo kple edzivɔ.
ENGLISH: For more than a decade, Frédéric Dumoulin has worked in the field of pharmaceutical research at Ghent University in Belgium.

EWE: Ɣeaɖeɣi va yi la, mexɔe se be Mawu li o.
ENGLISH: At one time he was an atheist.

EWE: Gake emegbe Frédéric va xɔe se be Mawue wɔ nu gbagbewo.
ENGLISH: But later Frédéric became convinced that God created life.

EWE: Nyɔ! magazinea talawo bia gbe Frédéric si nye Yehowa Ðasefo fifia tso eƒe xɔse kpakple eƒe dɔa ŋu.
ENGLISH: Awake! asked Frédéric who is now one of Jehovah’s Witnesses about his work and his faith.

EWE: Ðe wonyi wò le mawusubɔsubɔha aɖe mea?
ENGLISH: Did religion have any role in your childhood?
Yes.

EWE: Katolikotɔe danye nye.
ENGLISH: My mother was Roman Catholic.

EWE: Gake esi mexlẽ nu tso Atitsogaʋa kple Ŋutasẽʋɔnudɔdrɔ̃ ŋu la, mawusubɔsubɔ to le mo nam keŋkeŋ.
ENGLISH: But when I read about the Crusades and the Inquisition, I felt disgusted with religion and wanted nothing more to do with it.

EWE: Mexlẽ nu tso subɔsubɔha siwo mexɔ Kristo dzi se o hã ŋu, gake mekpɔe be tɔgã-tɔɖiviwo koe wo katã wonye.
ENGLISH: I also read about non-Christian religions and saw that they were no better.

EWE: Esi mexɔ ƒe 14 la, mese le ɖokuinye me be nu fitifiti wɔwɔ si bɔ ɖe subɔsubɔhawo me ɖo kpe edzi be Mawu meli o.
ENGLISH: When I was 14, I reasoned that the prevalence of corruption in religion proves that God doesn’t exist.

EWE: Eya ta esi wofia num tso nɔnɔmetɔtrɔ ŋu le suku la, melɔ̃ ɖe edzi be nu siwo me agbe me le o woe trɔ ʋuu va zu nu gbagbewo.
ENGLISH: So when I was taught the evolution theory at school, I concluded that life originated by natural processes.

EWE: Nu kae na nèva tsɔ ɖe le dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunya me?
ENGLISH: How were you attracted to science?

EWE: Esi mexɔ ƒe adre la, wona nusuekpɔmɔ̃m eye wòva zu nye fefenu vevitɔ.
ENGLISH: When I was seven, I was given a microscope and it became my favorite toy.

EWE: Metsɔnɛ léa ŋku ɖe nudzodzoevi lédzinamewo abe kpakpaluʋui ene ŋu.
ENGLISH: Among other things, I used it to examine fascinating insects, such as butterflies.

EWE: Aleke wòdzɔe be nèva tsɔ ɖe le ale si nu gbagbewo wɔ va dzɔ me?
ENGLISH: How did you become interested in the origin of life?

EWE: Esi mexɔ ƒe 22 la, medo go Yehowa Ðasefo aɖe si nye dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyala.
ENGLISH: When I was 22, I met a scientist who was one of Jehovah’s Witnesses.

EWE: Exɔe se be Mawue wɔ nu gbagbewo.
ENGLISH: She believed that God created life.

EWE: Esia wɔ moya nam ŋutɔ.
ENGLISH: That seemed really strange to me.

EWE: Mesusui be mate ŋu ana wòakpɔe be bometsitsie eƒe dzixɔse ma nye.
ENGLISH: I thought I could easily prove her faith to be ridiculous.

EWE: Gake nukutɔe la, eɖo nye nyabiasewo ŋu nam wòde edeƒe.
ENGLISH: But to my surprise, she had sensible answers to my questions.

EWE: Meva nɔ ŋugble dem tso ame siwo xɔ Mawu dzi se la ƒe nuwɔnawo ŋu.
ENGLISH: I became curious about people who believe in God.

EWE: Le ɣleti ʋɛ aɖewo megbe la, megado go Ðasefo bubu si hã nya nu tso atikewɔnyawo ŋu.
ENGLISH: A few months later, I met another Witness who was quite knowledgeable about medical matters.

EWE: Esi wòbe yeaƒo nu tso yeƒe dzixɔsewo ŋu nam la, melɔ̃ elabena medi be manya nu si tae amewo xɔ Mawu dzi se.
ENGLISH: When he offered to explain what he believed, I accepted his offer because I wanted to know why people believe in God.

EWE: Medi be maɖe fuflugba si wòdo na eɖokui la ɖa le ta nɛ.
ENGLISH: I wanted to save him from his delusion.

EWE: Ðe nète ŋu na wòkpɔe be ɖe woflu yea?
ENGLISH: Did you convince him that he was mistaken?

EWE: Ao.
ENGLISH: No, I didn’t.

EWE: Eya ta meva te nusɔsrɔ̃ tso nufiafia siwo ƒo nu tso ale si nu gbagbewo wɔ va dzɔ la ŋu.
ENGLISH: I began researching theories on the origin of life.

EWE: Nukutɔe la, meva kpɔe be dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyala xɔŋkɔ aɖewo gblɔ be lãmenugbagbevi suetɔ kekeake gɔ̃ hã ƒe wɔwɔme de ŋgɔ ale gbegbe be mate ŋu adzɔ le eɖokui si le anyigba sia dzi o.
ENGLISH: To my surprise, I found that some eminent scientists say that even the simplest living cell is so complex that it couldn’t have originated on earth.

EWE: Wo dometɔ aɖewo xɔe se be yamenutowo mee lãmenugbagbevi mawo dzɔ tso.
ENGLISH: Some of them think such cells came from outer space.

EWE: Woƒe nu mesɔ kura le ale si nu gbagbewo wɔ va dzɔ ŋu o.
ENGLISH: There is a lot of disagreement about how life began.

EWE: Ekema ɖe woƒe nu sɔ le nane ya mea?
ENGLISH: Is there a point of agreement?

EWE: Ewɔ moya be dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyala geɖe da asi ɖe edzi be le mɔ aɖe nu la, dzɔdzɔmenu siwo me agbe mele o lae trɔ ʋuu va zu nu gbagbewo.
ENGLISH: Strangely, many scientists agree that somehow natural processes caused life to spring from nonliving matter.

EWE: Meva nɔ ɖokuinye biam be: ‘Ne wobe ɖeko agbe dzɔ le eɖokui si evɔ womenya ale si wòdzɔe o la, ke nu kae na woka ɖe edzi alea gbegbe be nenema wòdzɔe?’
ENGLISH: I began to wonder, ‘If they don’t know how life could come about without a Creator, how can they be so sure that it happened that way?’

EWE: Meva nɔ nu si Biblia gblɔ tso ale si nu gbagbewo wɔ va dzɔ la ŋu bum vevie.
ENGLISH: I began to look into what the Bible says about the origin of life.

EWE: Aleke nèkpɔ Biblia ƒe nyawoe?
ENGLISH: What conclusions did you draw about the Bible?

EWE: Zi ale si meva le nu srɔ̃m tso Biblia ŋui la, zi nenemae mekana ɖe edzi be emenyawo nye nyateƒe.
ENGLISH: The more I learned from the Bible, the more I became convinced that it’s true.

EWE: Le kpɔɖeŋu me, nyitsɔ laa hafi dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyalawo va kpɔe dze sii be gɔmedzedze li na xexe gbahoo sia.
ENGLISH: For example, only recently have scientists found evidence that the universe had a beginning.

EWE: Gake Biblia ƒe kpukpui gbãtɔ si woŋlɔ ƒe 3,500 aɖewoe nye esia gblɔ be: "Le gɔmedzedzea me Mawu wɔ dziƒo kple anyigba. "
ENGLISH: But the opening verse of the Bible, written some 3,500 years ago, says: "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. "

EWE: Meva kpɔe be ne Biblia gblɔ nya aɖe tso dzɔdzɔmenuwo ŋu la, nenema tututu wònɔna.
ENGLISH: And I found that whenever the Bible comments on scientific matters, it is accurate.

EWE: Meva kpɔe be ne Biblia gblɔ nya aɖe tso dzɔdzɔmenuwo ŋu la, nenema tututu wònɔna
ENGLISH: I found that whenever the Bible comments on scientific matters, it is accurate

EWE: Ðe wòsesẽna na wò be nàxɔ Mawu dzi ase le esi nènye dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyala ta?
ENGLISH: Did your knowledge of science make believing in God difficult?

EWE: Kpao!
ENGLISH: No.

EWE: Ɣeyiɣi si me meva xɔ Mawu dzi se la, menɔ nu srɔ̃m tso dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunya ŋu anɔ abe ƒe etɔ̃e nye ema ene.
ENGLISH: When I first came to believe in God, I had been studying science at a university for three years.

EWE: Va se ɖe fifia la, zi ale si mele nu srɔ̃m tso nu gbagbewo ƒe wɔwɔme ŋu la, zi nenemae mexɔnɛ sena be Wɔla aɖe li.
ENGLISH: To this day, the more I study the design of living things, the more I am convinced that there is a Creator.

EWE: Àte ŋu ana eƒe kpɔɖeŋu aɖe mía?
ENGLISH: Can you give us an example?
Yes.

EWE: Mesrɔ̃ nu tso ŋusẽ si atikewo kple aɖinuwo kpɔna ɖe nu gbagbewo dzi la ŋu.
ENGLISH: I’ve studied the effects of medications and toxins on living creatures.

EWE: Nu si wɔ dɔ ɖe dzinye wue nye ale si aɖinuwo kple nugbagbevi gblẽnuwo metea ŋu gena ɖe míaƒe ahɔhɔ̃ me o.
ENGLISH: A design that impresses me is how our brain is protected from dangerous substances and from bacteria.

EWE: Nane li si tso míaƒe ʋu kple lãmenugbagbevi siwo le ahɔhɔ̃a me la dome.
ENGLISH: There is a barrier that keeps our blood separate from our brain cells.

EWE: Nu kae wɔ nuku le nu ma ŋu?
ENGLISH: What is remarkable about that?

EWE: Anɔ abe ƒe alafa ɖeka kple edzivɔ aɖewoe nye esia la, numekulawo de dzesii be nu siwo gena ɖe míaƒe ʋu me la yina ɖe ŋutilã ƒe akpa sia akpa negbe ahɔhɔ̃ kple dzimeƒuka koe do le eme.
ENGLISH: Over a hundred years ago, researchers noticed that substances introduced into the bloodstream enter every area of the body except the brain and spinal cord.

EWE: Nu ma wɔ nuku nam ŋutɔ elabe ʋuka wuwlui gbogbo aɖewoe tsɔa ʋu yina na lãmenugbagbevi ɖe sia ɖe si le ahɔhɔ̃a me.
ENGLISH: That fact is astonishing to me, because an immense network of tiny capillary vessels takes blood to every cell in the brain.

EWE: Ʋua klɔa lãmenugbagbevi siwo katã le ahɔhɔ̃a me la, eye ʋua kee naa nuɖuɖu kple ɔksidzin wo.
ENGLISH: All brain cells are cleaned, fed, and oxygenated by blood.

EWE: Ke aleke wòdzɔe be ʋua megena ɖe lãmenugbagbevi siwo le ahɔhɔ̃a me la me o?
ENGLISH: So, how can our blood be kept separate from our brain cells?

EWE: Ƒe geɖewoe nye esia womenya ale si tututu esia dzɔnae o.
ENGLISH: For many years it was a mystery. How does the barrier work?

EWE: Nu kae xea mɔ na ʋua be megena ɖe lãmenugbagbevi siwo le ahɔhɔ̃a me la me o? Ʋuka wuwlui siwo le ahɔhɔ̃a me mele abe aŋenuwo ene o.
ENGLISH: Microscopic blood vessels are not like plastic tubes that keep what’s inside separate from what’s outside.

EWE: Lãmenugbagbeviwo le ʋuka mawo ŋuti.
ENGLISH: The walls of blood vessels are made of cells.

EWE: Lãmenugbagbevi mawo ɖea mɔ nu ƒomevi aɖewo kple nugbagbevi nyaŋuinyaŋuiwo gena ɖe wo me alo zɔna le wo dome.
ENGLISH: These cells allow substances and microbes to pass through them and between them.

EWE: Ke hã, lãmenugbagbevi siwo le míaƒe ahɔhɔ̃ ƒe ʋukawo ŋu ya to vovovo kura.
ENGLISH: However, the cells making up the blood vessels in our brain are different.

EWE: Wotigi ɖe wo nɔewo ŋu.
ENGLISH: They’re tightly connected to each other.

EWE: Lãmenugbagbevi siawo kple woƒe kpeƒewo wɔ nuku.
ENGLISH: These cells and the tight junctions between them are amazing.

EWE: Nu siawo tea ŋu ɖea mɔ nanewo abe ɔksidzin, karbɔn-ya kple ʋumesukli toa ʋukawo me gena ɖe wo me le ɖoɖo nu.
ENGLISH: A vast array of complex mechanisms ensure that some things such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, and glucose pass between the bloodstream and the brain in a regulated way.

EWE: Gake meɖea mɔ nu bubuwo abe protein kple lãmenugbagbevi bubuwo gena ɖe eme o.
ENGLISH: But other compounds, proteins, and cells are kept out.

EWE: Eya ta nu si xea mɔ na ʋua be megena ɖe ahɔhɔ̃a me o la nyea molecule si xea mɔ na lãmenu vovovowo.
ENGLISH: So the blood-brain barrier operates at a molecular level to produce physical, chemical, and electrical barriers.

EWE: Nye ya mekpɔe be nu ma mate ŋu adzɔ le eɖokui si o.
ENGLISH: For me, such design simply could not have evolved.

EWE: Nu Gbagbewo Ŋuti Nunyala Aɖe Ƒe Xɔse

ENGLISH: Dr. Hans Kristian Kotlar

EWE: Ɣemaɣi la, eva di vevie be yeanya ale si nu gbagbewo wɔ va dzɔ.
ENGLISH: At that time, he also became interested in the origin of life.

ENGLISH: Awake! asked him about his research and his religious faith.

EWE: Nu kae na nètsɔ ɖe le ale si nu gbagbewo wɔ va dzɔ kple nu si tae míele agbe ɖo la me?
ENGLISH: What stirred your interest in the origin and meaning of life?

EWE: Tɔ́nye nye Katolikotɔ eye Nɔnye nye Protestanttɔ.
ENGLISH: My father was Catholic and my mother was Protestant.

EWE: Gake wometsɔa mawusubɔsubɔ nu vevie o.
ENGLISH: That said, they did not view religion as important.

EWE: Esime menye ŋutsuvi dzaa la, medea ŋugble tso nu si tae míele agbe ɖo la ŋu, eye mexlẽ agbalẽwo tso Buddha Subɔsubɔha, Hindu Subɔsubɔha kple Islam Subɔsubɔha ŋu.
ENGLISH: As for me, during my teens, I wondered about the meaning of life, and I read books about Buddhism, Hinduism, and Islam.

EWE: Mebia Mawu gɔ̃ hã kpɔ be wòana manya nyateƒe la.
ENGLISH: I even asked God to reveal the truth to me.

EWE: Le ƒe 1970 ƒe ƒeawo me la, wova wɔ ŋgɔyiyi ɖedzesi geɖewo le lãmenugbagbeviwo ŋuti nunya me, eye mesusui be esia ate ŋu ana woava nya ale si nu gbagbewo wɔ va dzɔ.
ENGLISH: By the 1970’s, the field of molecular biology had made some amazing advances, and I wondered if it might reveal how life began.

EWE: Nu gbagbewo ƒe lãmenugbagbeviwo ƒe wɔwɔme wɔ dɔ ɖe dzinye ŋutɔ, eya ta metiae be masrɔ̃ nu tso nu gbagbewo ŋu.
ENGLISH: The mechanisms within living cells intrigued me, so I chose to study biotechnology.

EWE: Gakpe ɖe eŋu la, nufialawo dometɔ akpa gãtɔ gblɔna be ɖe nuwo dzɔ le wo ɖokuiwo si, eye mexɔ woƒe nyawo dzi se.
ENGLISH: I might add that most of my professors said that life evolved by natural processes, and I believed them.

EWE: Nu ka tae nètsɔ ɖe le Biblia me?
ENGLISH: Why did you take an interest in the Bible?

EWE: Yehowa Ðasefo eve va míaƒe aƒe me gbe ɖeka.
ENGLISH: Two of Jehovah’s Witnesses visited our home.

EWE: Togbɔ be wodo vivi ɖe ŋunye hã la, meblu ɖe wo ta, eye megblɔ be nyemedi be mase woƒe nyawo o.
ENGLISH: Although they were pleasant, I reacted rudely and told them I was not interested. My wife overheard me.

EWE: Srɔ̃nye se mía ŋkɔ, eye wògblɔ nam be: "Srɔ̃nye Hans Kristian, mèwɔe nyuie o.
ENGLISH: "That was not kind, Hans Kristian, " she said.

EWE: Menye wòe dina be yeanya nu si ta míele agbe ɖo oa? "
ENGLISH: "You have always been interested in the meaning of life. "

EWE: Mekpɔe be eƒe nya le eme; ŋu kpem.
ENGLISH: She was right, and I felt ashamed.

EWE: Ale wɔ mesi du dze Ðasefoawo yome.
ENGLISH: So I ran after the Witnesses.

EWE: Esi míenɔ dze ɖom la, megblɔ na wo be medi be manya nenye be Biblia wɔ ɖeka kple dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunya.
ENGLISH: During our conversation, I told them that I wanted to know if the Bible is in harmony with science.

EWE: Aleke wowɔ nui?
ENGLISH: How did they respond to that?

EWE: Woxlẽ nya si Biblia gblɔ tso afi si dzɔdzɔmeŋusẽ si le xexea me la dzɔ tso la ŋu nam.
ENGLISH: They showed me what the Bible says about the Source of the energy manifest in the universe.

EWE: Ðe wòle be woabia nya geɖe tso nufiafia sia ŋu hafi.
ENGLISH: I think they should ask more questions.

EWE: Nu ka tae nèva zu Yehowa Ðasefo?
ENGLISH: Why did you become one of Jehovah’s Witnesses?

EWE: Yehowa Ðasefowo ƒe amedzrowɔwɔ kple ale si woxɔ ŋugbe si Wɔlaa do ku ɖe etsɔme nyui aɖe ŋu dzi se la wɔ dɔ ɖe dzinye ŋutɔ.
ENGLISH: I was attracted by their hospitality and their faith in the Creator’s promise of a better future.

EWE: Ðe wokua nyawo me tsitotsito hekpɔa kpeɖodzi na wo hafi xɔa wo dzi sena, ke menye nyakpakpa alo nususugblɔwo dzie woxɔna sena o.
ENGLISH: And that faith rests on research and sound reasoning, not myths or speculation.

ENGLISH: Dr. Feng-Ling Yang

ENGLISH: Feng-Ling Yang is a senior research assistant at the central research academy in Taipei, Taiwan.

EWE: Wota nu siwo ŋu wòke ɖo la ɖe dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunya ƒe agbalẽwo me.
ENGLISH: Her work has been published in scientific journals.

EWE: Tsã la, exɔ nufiafia si nye be ɖeko nuwo dzɔ le wo ɖokui si la dzi se.
ENGLISH: She used to believe in the theory of evolution.

ENGLISH: But then she changed her mind.

ENGLISH: Awake! asked her about her science and her faith.

ENGLISH: We raised pigs and grew vegetables in a flood-prone area near the city of Taipei.

EWE: Dzinyelawo fia nu si tae wòle vevie be manye dɔ sesẽ wɔla lam eye wofiam hã be makpe ɖe amewo ŋu.
ENGLISH: My parents taught me the value of hard work, and they also taught me to help other people.

EWE: Mawusubɔlawoe dziwòlawo nyea?
ENGLISH: Was your family religious?

EWE: Dzinyelawo nye Tao-subɔsubɔha me tɔwo.
ENGLISH: My family practiced Taoism.

EWE: Míesaa vɔ na "Dziƒo Mawu " la, gake míenya naneke tso eŋu o.
ENGLISH: We made sacrifices to the "Heaven God, " but we didn’t know anything about him.

EWE: Mebiaa ɖokuinye be: ‘Nu ka tae amewo ɖua aya?
ENGLISH: I used to wonder: ‘Why do people suffer?

EWE: Nu ka tae amewo dia wo ɖokuiwo tɔ?’
ENGLISH: Why are people selfish?’

EWE: Mexlẽ agbalẽ geɖe tso Tao-subɔsubɔha, Buddha-subɔsubɔha kpakple Europatɔwo kple Amerikatɔwo ƒe ŋutinyawo ŋu.
ENGLISH: I read books about Taoism and Buddhism and about Eastern and Western history.

EWE: Mede sɔleme geɖewo gɔ̃ hã.
ENGLISH: I even went to a couple of churches.

EWE: Gake nyemete ŋu kpɔ nye nyabiaseawo ƒe ŋuɖoɖowo o.
ENGLISH: But I couldn’t find answers to my questions.

EWE: Nu ka tae nèsrɔ̃ dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunya?
ENGLISH: Why did you study science?

EWE: Melɔ̃ akɔntabubu, eye se siwo fiaa mɔ ɖoɖo si nu dzɔdzɔmenuwo nɔna la wɔa dɔ ɖe dzinye ŋutɔ.
ENGLISH: I liked mathematics and was fascinated by the way physical and chemical laws govern the structure of things.

EWE: Se aɖewoe fiaa mɔ ɖoɖo si nu nuwɔwɔ ɖe sia ɖe wɔa dɔ le, tso xexeme gbahoo sia dzi va se ɖe nugbagbevi suetɔ kekeake dzi.
ENGLISH: Everything, from the immense universe to tiny microbes, has a structure that is controlled by rules.

EWE: Medi vevie be mase ale si se siawo wɔa dɔe la gɔme.
ENGLISH: And I wanted to understand those rules.

EWE: Nu ka tae nèxɔ nufiafia si nye be ɖeko nuwo dzɔ le wo ɖokuiwo si la dzi se tsã?
ENGLISH: Why did you believe the theory of evolution to be a fact?

EWE: Nyemesrɔ̃ naneke si tsi tre ɖe nufiafia sia ŋu kpɔ o.
ENGLISH: I was taught nothing to the contrary.

ENGLISH: And then because of being a researcher in a life science, I was expected to accept evolution.

EWE: Esi wònye mekua nu me tso nu gbagbewo ŋu ta la, ele nam be maxɔ nufiafia si nye be ɖeko nuwo dzɔ le wo ɖokuiwo si la dzi se
ENGLISH: Because I was a researcher in a life science, I was expected to accept evolution

ENGLISH: What made you start reading the Bible?

EWE: Meʋu yi ɖatsi Germany le ƒe 1996 me be masrɔ̃ nu ayi ŋgɔe le nye yunivɛsitiɖaseɖigbalẽ gbãtɔ xɔxɔ megbe.
ENGLISH: I went to live in Germany in 1996 to start my postgraduate studies.

EWE: Le ƒe si kplɔe ɖo me la, medo go aƒenɔ aɖe si ŋkɔe nye Simone.
ENGLISH: The following year I met a lady named Simone.

EWE: Yehowa Ðasefoe wònye, eye egblɔ be yeakpe ɖe ŋunye makpɔ ŋuɖoɖo na nye nyabiasewo le Biblia me.
ENGLISH: She was one of Jehovah’s Witnesses, and she offered to show me the Bible’s answers to my questions.

EWE: Esi wògblɔ nam be Biblia gblɔ nu si ta míele agbe ɖo la, ewɔ dɔ ɖe dzinye ale gbegbe.
ENGLISH: When she told me that the Bible explains the purpose of life, I was intrigued.

EWE: Esia ta mefɔna fɔŋli ga ene kple afã gbe sia gbe xlẽa Biblia gaƒoƒo ɖeka sɔŋ.
ENGLISH: I began getting up at half past four each morning to read the Bible for an hour.

EWE: Eyome menɔa zɔzɔm le nutoa me henɔa ŋugble dem le nu siwo mexlẽ ŋu.
ENGLISH: Then I would go for a walk to meditate.

EWE: Le ƒe si kplɔe me la, mexlẽ Biblia katã vɔ.
ENGLISH: During the next year, I read the whole Bible.

EWE: Ale si Biblia me nyagblɔɖiwo va eme pɛpɛpɛ la wɔ dɔ ɖe dzinye ŋutɔ.
ENGLISH: I was impressed by the accuracy of its prophecies.

EWE: Vivivi la, meva ka ɖe edzi bliboe be Mawu gbɔe Biblia la tso.
ENGLISH: Gradually, I became convinced that the Bible is from God.

ENGLISH: Well, when I began giving this serious thought in the late 1990’s, molecular biologists were beginning to realize that the chemistry of life is much more elaborate than anyone had previously thought.

EWE: Enye nyateƒe be dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyalawo nyae tso gbe aɖe gbe ke be nunyiame siwo le nu gbagbewo ƒe lãmenugbagbeviwo me la ƒe wɔwɔme kple dɔwɔwɔ gɔme sese sesẽ wu molecule ɖe sia ɖe si li la tɔ.
ENGLISH: Of course, scientists had long known that the proteins in living cells are the most chemically sophisticated molecules in existence.

EWE: Gake fifia la, wova nya nu tso ale si protein gbogbo aɖewo ƒua ƒu wɔa mɔ̃ siwo ƒe akpa aɖewo zɔna la ŋu.
ENGLISH: But now, they were discovering how whole assemblies of proteins are organized to form elegant machines with moving parts.

EWE: Protein 50 kple edzivɔwo ƒoa ƒu wɔa molecule-mɔ̃ ɖeka.
ENGLISH: A molecular machine might be composed of over 50 proteins.

EWE: Le kpɔɖeŋu me, ehiã mɔ̃ sia be wòatsɔ awɔ ŋusẽ, agbugbɔ nyatakakawo aŋlɔ alo be wòadzɔ mɔnu vovovo siwo le lãmenugbagbevia ŋuti la nu.
ENGLISH: And even the simplest cell needs a collection of different machines for example, to generate power, to duplicate information, and to control access across membranes.

ENGLISH: What did you conclude?

EWE: Mebia ɖokuinye be, ‘Aleke wòdzɔe be protein-mɔ̃ mawo de ŋgɔ nenema gbegbe?’
ENGLISH: Well, I asked myself, ‘How did those protein machines become so well engineered?’

ENGLISH: At the time, the unexpected complexity of cell chemistry made a number of scientists ask the same question.

EWE: Lãmetsiŋutinunyalagã aɖe si le United States ta agbalẽ aɖe si ɖe nu me be molecule-mɔ̃ siwo le lãmenugbagbeviwo me de ŋgɔ ale gbegbe be womate ŋu adzɔ le wo ɖokuiwo si o.
ENGLISH: A professor of biochemistry in the United States published a book arguing that the molecular machines in living cells are so complex that they could not have originated randomly.

ENGLISH: I agreed.

EWE: Mekpɔe be ame aɖe kokokoe wɔ nu gbagbewo.
ENGLISH: I felt that life must have been created.

EWE: Mebia ɖokuinye be, ‘Aleke wòdzɔe be protein-mɔ̃ mawo de ŋgɔ nenema gbegbe?’
ENGLISH: I asked myself, ‘How did those protein machines become so well engineered?’

ENGLISH: Why did you become one of Jehovah’s Witnesses?

ENGLISH: I was impressed that although Simone had health problems, she traveled some 35 miles (56 km) each week to teach me the Bible.

ENGLISH: I learned that during Germany’s Nazi era, some Witnesses were imprisoned in concentration camps for their political neutrality.

EWE: Eye ale si dzi nɔ wo ƒoe hã wɔ dɔ ɖe dzinye ŋutɔ.
ENGLISH: Their courage deeply impressed me.

EWE: Nenema kee ale si gbegbe Ðasefoawo lɔ̃ Mawui na meɖoe be manɔ abe woawo ke ene.

ENGLISH: Has believing in God benefited you?

ENGLISH: My colleagues say that I’m happier now.

EWE: Mɔ ka nue lãmenugbagbevi siwo le dɔ dzi le míaƒe lãme ƒe kuku ɖea vi le?
ENGLISH: In what way is programmed cell death vital?

EWE: Lãmenugbagbevi suesue siwo ŋku mate ŋu akpɔ o miliɔn teƒe miliɔn geɖe ye le míaƒe lãme.
ENGLISH: Well, our body is made up of trillions of microscopic cells.

EWE: Le ɖoɖoa nu la, ele be esiawo katã naku eye bubuwo naxɔ ɖe wo teƒe.
ENGLISH: Practically all of them must die and be replaced.

EWE: Lãmenugbagbevi siawo ƒe agbenɔƒewo le vovovo; ɖewo ɖɔlina le kwasiɖa ʋɛ aɖewo megbe eye bubuwo nɔa anyi ƒe ʋɛ aɖewo hafi kuna.
ENGLISH: Each type of cell has a different life span; some are replaced every few weeks, and others every few years.

EWE: Woƒe kuku kple wo ɖokui ɖɔliɖɔli zɔna ɖe ɖoɖo nyui aɖe ŋutɔ nu ale be wòagagblẽ naneke le mía ŋu o.
ENGLISH: Our body’s system of programmed cell death has to be highly controlled to maintain the delicate balance between cell death and cell formation.

EWE: Ke nu kae ate ŋu agblẽ nu le mía ŋu?
ENGLISH: What can go wrong?

EWE: Numekuku aɖewo ɖee fia be, ne ele be lãmenugbagbevi aɖe naku gake meku o la, ate ŋu ahe ƒunukpeƒetetedɔ kple kansa avɛ.
ENGLISH: Some studies indicate that when cells fail to die as they should, rheumatoid arthritis or cancer may result.

EWE: Azɔ hã, ne lãmenugbagbevi aɖe ku do ŋgɔ la, ate ŋu ahe lãmetutudɔ kple tsitsimedɔléle si gblẽa nu le ame ƒe susu ŋu avɛ.
ENGLISH: On the other hand, when cells die before they should, it could cause Parkinson’s disease or Alzheimer’s disease.

EWE: Nye numekukua ƒe akpa aɖee nye be madi ale si woada dɔ siawoe.
ENGLISH: My research is linked to finding ways to treat these diseases.

EWE: Vi kae nusɔsrɔ̃ tso ale si lãmenugbagbeviwo kuna ŋu ɖe na wò?
ENGLISH: How did your study of cell death affect you?

EWE: Le nyateƒe me la, ewɔ nuku nam.
ENGLISH: Frankly, it puzzled me.

EWE: Mekpɔe be ame aɖe si di be míanɔ lãmesẽ me kokokoe anya wɔ ɖoɖo nyui sia.
ENGLISH: This marvelous process was clearly designed by someone who wants us to be healthy.

EWE: Eya ta megabiaa ɖokuinye kokoko be, Nu ka tae amegbetɔwo kpea fu hekuna?
ENGLISH: So I was still left with the question, Why do people suffer and die?

EWE: Nyemekpɔ ŋuɖoɖoa o.
ENGLISH: I couldn’t find an answer.

EWE: Gake èva ka ɖe edzi be ame aɖee wɔ ɖoɖo be lãmenugbagbeviwo nanɔ wo nɔewo ɖɔlim ya.
ENGLISH: But you were convinced that the system of programmed cell death was designed.
Yes.

EWE: Ðoɖo bliboa gɔmesese mele bɔbɔe kura o, gake ale si lãmenu siawo wɔa dɔ le ɖoɖo nyui nu la ɖe nunya gã aɖe fia.
ENGLISH: The complexity of the whole process is mind-boggling, yet its elegance displays exceptional wisdom.

EWE: Meka ɖe edzi be Mawu ƒe nunyae.
ENGLISH: I believe it’s the wisdom of God.

EWE: Mezã nusuekpɔmɔ̃ be matsɔ ase ɖoɖo vovovo siwo nana lãmenugbagbevi siawo nɔa dɔ dzi la gɔme.
ENGLISH: I use powerful microscopes to study the many complex mechanisms that regulate the process.

EWE: Ðoɖo siawo dometɔ aɖewo tea ŋu ɖɔa nu ɖo le aɖabaƒoƒo ʋɛ aɖewo ko me ne ehiã.
ENGLISH: Some mechanisms can trigger the destruction process within seconds if need be.

EWE: Lãmenugbagbevi siawo ŋutɔe ɖea esiwo gblẽ la ɖa.
ENGLISH: The cells participate in their own self-destruction.

EWE: Wowɔ ɖoɖoa wòde ŋgɔ ale gbegbe be nu bliboa wɔ nuku ŋutɔ.
ENGLISH: The process is so well-designed that it’s absolutely awe-inspiring.

EWE: Esi míaƒe lãmenugbagbeviwo katã ɖɔa li wo nɔewo ɖe ɖoɖo nyui aɖe nu ta la, anya wɔ be míanɔ agbe tegbee
ENGLISH: Since nearly all our cells are regularly replaced, living forever is certainly feasible

EWE: Nyabiase aɖewo nɔ asiwò ku ɖe nu si tae Mawu ɖe mɔ ɖe fukpekpe ŋu.
ENGLISH: You had questions about God and suffering.

EWE: Aleke nèwɔ kpɔ ŋuɖoɖoawo?
ENGLISH: How did you find answers?

EWE: Le ƒe 1991 me la, atsu kple asi aɖe siwo nye Yehowa Ðasefowo va nye aƒe me, eye mebia be woaɖe nu si tae míekuna me nam.
ENGLISH: A couple of Jehovah’s Witnesses called at my home in 1991, and I asked them why we die.

EWE: Wotsɔ ale si Biblia ɖo nya sia ŋui la fiam: "To ame ɖeka dzi nu vɔ̃ ge ɖe xexea me, eye to nu vɔ̃ me ku la va. "
ENGLISH: They showed me the Bible’s answer: "Through one man sin entered into the world and death through sin. "

EWE: (Romatɔwo 5:12) Ne ɖe ame gbãtɔ ɖo to Mawu la, anye ne anɔ agbe tegbee.
ENGLISH: (Romans 5:12) If the first man had not disobeyed God, he would have lived forever.

EWE: Enumake mede dzesii be esia wɔ ɖeka kple nu siwo ŋu meke ɖo le nye numekukuwo me.
ENGLISH: I immediately realized that this harmonized with what I had learned from my research.

EWE: Eme va kɔ nam azɔ be Mawu mewɔ mí be míaku hafi o.
ENGLISH: In fact, it’s clear to me that God didn’t intend for people to die.

EWE: Esi míaƒe lãmenugbagbeviwo katã ɖɔa li wo nɔewo ɖe ɖoɖo nyui aɖe nu ta la, anya wɔ be míanɔ agbe tegbee.
ENGLISH: Since nearly all our cells are regularly replaced, living forever is certainly feasible.

EWE: Nu kae na nèva ka ɖe edzi be Mawu ƒe Nyae Biblia la nye?
ENGLISH: What convinced you that the Bible is God’s Word?

EWE: Meva srɔ̃ nu si Biblia gblɔ tso Mawu ŋu le Psalmo 139:16: ‘Esi menye ʋukɔe la, wò ŋkuwo kpɔm, eye woŋlɔ wo ɖe wò agbalẽ me.’
ENGLISH: I learned what the Bible says about God at Psalm 139:16: "Your eyes saw even the embryo of me, and in your book all its parts were down in writing. "

EWE: Esi menye lãmetsiŋutinunyala ta la, mesrɔ̃a nu tso ale si míaƒe lãmenugbagbeviwo wɔa dɔe ŋu.
ENGLISH: As a biochemist, I study the genetic information that is written in our cells.

EWE: Aleke ame si ŋlɔ Psalmowo wɔ nya esia?
ENGLISH: How did the psalmist know about such writing?

EWE: Zi ale si meyi Biblia sɔsrɔ̃ dzi la, zi nenemae meva ka ɖe edzi be Mawue na woŋlɔ Biblia.
ENGLISH: The more I learned from the Bible, the more I was convinced that it is inspired of God.

EWE: Aleke wokpe ɖe ŋuwò nèva se Biblia ƒe nufiafiawo gɔmee?
ENGLISH: How were you helped to understand what the Bible teaches?

EWE: Yehowa Ðasefo aɖe srɔ̃ Biblia kplim.
ENGLISH: One of Jehovah’s Witnesses offered to study the Bible with me.

EWE: Meva se nu si tae Mawu ɖe mɔ amegbetɔwo kpea fu ɖo la gɔme.
ENGLISH: Finally, I learned why God has allowed suffering.

EWE: Meva srɔ̃e, abe ale si Biblia ŋutɔ gblɔe ene, be Mawu do ŋugbe be ‘yeami ku saɖagatsi tegbee.’
ENGLISH: I also learned that, as the Bible states, God purposes to "swallow up death forever. "

EWE: (Yesaya 25:8) Ele bɔbɔe na mía Wɔla la be wòatrɔ asi le míaƒe ameti wɔnukua ŋu be wòayi edzi anɔ dɔ wɔm le ɖoɖo deblibo nu ale be míase vivi na agbe si nuwuwu manɔe na o.
ENGLISH: (Isaiah 25:8) It will be easy for our Creator to make the marvelous systems of our body operate perfectly so that we can enjoy life without end.

EWE: Aleke nèzã Biblia me nunya si su asiwò la tsɔ kpe ɖe amewo ŋui?
ENGLISH: How have you used your knowledge of the Bible to help others?

EWE: Meva zu Yehowa Ðasefo le ƒe 1995 me, eye tso ɣemaɣi la, meƒoa nu tso nu siwo mesrɔ̃ le Biblia me ŋu na amewo.
ENGLISH: Well, I became one of Jehovah’s Witnesses in 1995, and since then I have freely shared with others the things I’ve learned from the Bible.

EWE: Le kpɔɖeŋu me, nye dɔwɔhati aɖe ƒe dzi gbã vevie esime nɔviaŋutsu wu eɖokui.
ENGLISH: For example, a colleague of mine was devastated when her brother committed suicide.

EWE: Sɔleme si wòdena fiaa nu be Mawu matsɔ ame siwo wu wo ɖokui la ƒe nu vɔ̃ ake wo gbeɖe o.
ENGLISH: Her church teaches that God never forgives suicide.

EWE: Gake metsɔ ale si Biblia ƒo nu tso tsitretsitsi mɔkpɔkpɔa ŋu la fiae.
ENGLISH: But I showed her how the Bible gives a hope of a resurrection.

EWE: (Yohanes 5:28, 29) Eƒe dzi dze eme ŋutɔ esi wòva kpɔe be Wɔla la tsɔa ɖe le eme na mí.
ENGLISH: (John 5:28, 29) She was deeply comforted to learn that the Creator cares for us.

EWE: Le nɔnɔme siawo tɔgbi me la, mekpɔnɛ be Biblia me nyawo gbɔgblɔ na amewo nana mekpɔa dzidzɔ wu nu si dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunya si menya ate ŋu awɔ nam!
ENGLISH: At such moments, I feel that sharing Bible truths with others brings me more satisfaction than science itself!

EWE: Lãmetsiŋutinunyala Aɖe Ƒe Xɔse
ENGLISH: A Biochemist Explains His Faith

EWE: Ðɔkta Davey Loos nye lãmetsiŋutinunyala le Belgium.
ENGLISH: Dr. Davey Loos is a biochemist in Belgium.

EWE: Ɣeaɖeɣi va yi la, mexɔe se be Wɔla aɖe li o, ke boŋ exɔe se be ɖeko nuwo dzɔ le wo ɖokuiwo si.
ENGLISH: At one time, he doubted the existence of a Creator, believing instead in evolution.

EWE: Gake eva trɔ susu emegbe.
ENGLISH: Later, he changed his mind.

EWE: Nu kae na ɖɔkta sia gbugbɔ ŋku lé ɖe eƒe dzixɔse ku ɖe ale si nu gbagbewo wɔ va dzɔ la ŋu?
ENGLISH: What caused a researcher to reconsider his beliefs about the origin of life?

EWE: Nyɔ! magazinea talawo bia gbee tso eƒe xɔse kpakple eƒe dɔa ŋu.
ENGLISH: Awake! asked Dr. Loos about his science and his faith.

EWE: Aleke nèwɔ va zu dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyala?
ENGLISH: How did you become involved in scientific research?

EWE: Esi menɔ yunivɛsiti la, mesrɔ̃ lãmetsiŋutinunya.
ENGLISH: When I attended university, I chose to study chemistry.

EWE: Nu siwo wɔ dɔ ɖe dzinye vevie nye protein kple nucleic acid siwo de ŋgɔ sãsãsã wu molecule ɖe sia ɖe le anyigba dzi.
ENGLISH: I was particularly fascinated by proteins and nucleic acids, which are by far the most complex molecules on our planet.

EWE: Gake ale si molecule aɖewo wɔa nui ne ɣe klẽ ɖe wo dzi la wɔa nuku nam ŋutɔ.
ENGLISH: In time, I became intrigued by the way certain molecules respond to sunlight.

EWE: Ðe nèxɔ Mawu dzi se tsãa?
ENGLISH: Did you believe in God?

EWE: Mexɔ Mawu dzi se esime menɔ ɖevime.
ENGLISH: I did when I was a little boy.

EWE: Gake esi meva nɔ suku dem le Catholic University le Leuven la, wofiam be dzɔdzɔmenuwoe nɔ tɔtrɔm vivivi va zu nu gbagbewo.
ENGLISH: But later, while I was studying at the Catholic University of Leuven, I was taught that living things owe their designs to natural processes.

EWE: Ale si nufialagã siawo ɖea dzɔdzɔmenuwo ƒe tɔtrɔ siawo dometɔ aɖewo gɔme la wɔa dɔ ɖe dzinye ŋutɔ.
ENGLISH: The professors made some of these processes sound quite complicated.

EWE: Esi wònye dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyala kpɔnuteƒewoe wonye ta la, mexɔ woƒe nyawo dzi se.
ENGLISH: They were experienced scientists, so I believed what they said.

EWE: Mlɔeba la, eva sesẽ nam be maxɔe ase be Mawu li.
ENGLISH: Eventually, I found it difficult to accept the existence of God.

EWE: Nu kae na nègbugbɔ ŋku lé ɖe nu gbagbewo ƒe dzɔtsoƒe ŋu?
ENGLISH: What made you reconsider the origin of life?

EWE: Le ƒe 1999 me la, medo go xɔ̃nye aɖe si nye kplii míede suku si va zu Yehowa Ðasefo, eye mede woƒe kpekpeawo dometɔ ɖeka.
ENGLISH: In 1999, I met a friend from my school days who had become one of Jehovah’s Witnesses, and I attended one of their meetings.

EWE: Ɣemaɣi la, Yehowa Ðasefo aɖe va mía ƒe me eye wòna agbalẽ si nye Is There a Creator Who Cares About You? (Y a-t-il un Créateur qui se soucie de vous?) ɖekam.
ENGLISH: Also about that time, one of Jehovah’s Witnesses visited our house and left a copy of the book Is There a Creator Who Cares About You?

EWE: Nu kae nèsusu tso agbalẽa ŋu?
ENGLISH: What did you think about the book?

EWE: Ale si woku nu me memie hafi tae la wɔ dɔ ɖe dzinye.
ENGLISH: I was impressed by the quality of the research that it presented.

EWE: Esia na meva nɔ eŋu bum nenye be nu siwo le xexea me la woate ŋu adzɔ le wo ɖokuiwo si vavã.
ENGLISH: I began to wonder if evolution really did explain the designs seen in nature.

EWE: Nuwɔwɔ siwo le xexea me la dometɔ kae wɔ nuku na wò wu?
ENGLISH: What designs in nature impressed you?

EWE: Esi menye lãmetsiŋutinunyala ta la, mesrɔ̃ nu tso molecule siwo le cyanobacteria siwo le atsiaƒu me la ŋu, siwo nye nugbagbevi suesuesue siwo wɔa woawo ŋutɔwo ƒe nuɖuɖuwo eye womekpɔa woƒe nuɖuɖu tso nu gbagbe bubu aɖeke gbɔ o.
ENGLISH: My work as a biochemist involved studying the design of certain molecules found in ocean-dwelling cyanobacteria, which are microorganisms that don’t depend on other living things for food.

EWE: Numekula aɖewo susui be nugbagbevi suesuesue siawoe nye nu gbagbe gbãtɔ siwo nɔ anyigba dzi.
ENGLISH: Some researchers think that these organisms were the first living things on our planet.

EWE: Wowɔa ŋusẽ si tso ɣe ƒe dzoxɔxɔ gbɔ ŋu dɔ tsɔ trɔa tsi kple ya si woyɔna be carbon dioxide wozua nuɖuɖu na wo, eye ale si wowɔa nu siae la gɔme sese sesẽ ŋutɔ.
ENGLISH: Using energy from sunlight, the microbes use an extremely complex chemical process, which is still not fully understood, to convert water and carbon dioxide into food.

EWE: Ale si cyanobacteria tea ŋu wɔna kpɔa ɣe ƒe keklẽ si dena nɛ la hã wɔa nuku nam ŋutɔ.
ENGLISH: I was also amazed at how cyanobacteria can harvest light with incredible efficiency.

EWE: Aŋgbawo hã trɔa ɣe ƒe kekeli wòzua nuɖuɖu na wo.
ENGLISH: Leaves also use sunlight to make food.

EWE: Eya ta mɔ ka nue nugbagbevi sia tɔ ɖe dzesi le?
ENGLISH: So, what is remarkable about those bacteria?

EWE: Ɣe ƒe keklẽ vi aɖe koe tea ŋu ɖoa atsiaƒu gɔme.
ENGLISH: The deeper you go in the sea, the less light you find.

EWE: Eya ta ele na nugbagbevi si nye cyanobacteria, si nɔa atsiaƒu gɔme la be wòalé ɣe ƒe keklẽ sue ɖe sia ɖe si wòkpɔ la ɖi eye wòzãa ŋusẽxɔti deŋgɔ aɖe tsɔ wɔa esia.
ENGLISH: So the cyanobacteria that live there must capture every scrap of light energy that comes their way, and they do this by means of highly sophisticated antennae.

EWE: Etrɔa ŋusẽ si wòlé ɖi la katã kloe wòzua nuɖuɖu.
ENGLISH: The collected energy is transmitted to food-producing centers with nearly 100 percent efficiency.

EWE: Ale si nugbagbevi sia tea ŋu léa ɣe ƒe keklẽ ɖi la wɔa nuku na ame siwo wɔa elektrik-namɔ̃ siwo zãa ɣe ƒe keklẽ ale gbegbe be wova tsɔ ɖe le eme vevie.
ENGLISH: The design of this light-harvesting machinery has even attracted the interest of solar-panel manufacturers.

EWE: Ke hã, ale si nugbagbevi sia wɔna léa ɣe ƒe keklẽ ɖi la de ŋgɔ sãsãsã wu elektrik-namɔ̃ siwo zãa ɣe ƒe keklẽ.
ENGLISH: Of course, manufactured solar cells are nowhere near as efficient as the systems found in bacteria.

EWE: Nya ta kae esia na nèƒo?
ENGLISH: What did that cause you to conclude?

EWE: Mede ŋugble tso mɔ̃ɖaŋudɔwɔla siwo dze agbagba srɔ̃ nu wɔnuku siwo yia edzi le nu gbagbewo me la ŋu eye meƒo nya ta be Mawu kokokoe wɔ nu gbagbewo
ENGLISH: I thought about engineers trying to imitate the marvelous mechanisms found in living things, and I came to the conclusion that life must have been designed by God

EWE: Mede ŋugble tso mɔ̃ɖaŋudɔwɔla siwo dze agbagba srɔ̃ nu wɔnuku siwo yia edzi le nu gbagbewo me la ŋu eye meƒo nya ta be Mawu kokokoe wɔ nu gbagbewo.
ENGLISH: I thought about engineers trying to imitate the marvelous mechanisms found in living things, and I came to the conclusion that life must have been designed by God.

EWE: Gake menye nu siwo mesrɔ̃ le dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunya me koe na meva xɔe se be Mawu li o.
ENGLISH: But my faith was not based solely on what I studied in science.

EWE: Biblia sɔsrɔ̃ veviedodotɔe hã kpe ɖe ŋunye.
ENGLISH: It was also based on a careful study of the Bible.

EWE: Nu kae na nèka ɖe edzi be Mawu gbɔe Biblia tso?
ENGLISH: What convinced you that the Bible is from God?

EWE: Nu siwo na meka ɖe edzi la dometɔ ɖekae nye ale si Biblia me nyagblɔɖiwo vaa eme pɛpɛpɛ.
ENGLISH: One of the many things that convinced me was the detailed fulfillment of Bible prophecies.

ENGLISH: For example, centuries in advance Isaiah described in abundant detail the death and burial of Jesus.

ENGLISH: We know this prophecy was written before Jesus’ death because the Isaiah Scroll, found at Qumran, was copied about a hundred years before Jesus was born.

EWE: Nyagblɔɖi ma gblɔ be: "Woɖe yɔdo nɛ ɖe ame vɔ̃ɖiwo dome eye le eƒe ku me wòmlɔ kesinɔtɔwo dome. "
ENGLISH: That prophecy says: "He will make his burial place even with the wicked ones, and with the rich class in his death. "

EWE: (Yesaya 53:9, 12, Agbenya La) Nukutɔe la, wowu Yesu abe ame vɔ̃ɖi ene, gake woɖii ɖe kesinɔtɔwo ƒe ƒome aɖe ƒe yɔdo me.
ENGLISH: (Isaiah 53:9, 12) Remarkably, Jesus was executed with criminals but was buried in the tomb of a wealthy family.

EWE: Esia nye nyagblɔɖi gbogbo siwo va eme, siwo na meka ɖe edzi be Mawu ƒe gbɔgbɔe ʋã amewo woŋlɔ Biblia la dometɔ ɖeka ko.
ENGLISH: This is just one example of the many fulfilled prophecies that convinced me that the Bible is inspired of God.

EWE: (2 Timoteo 3:16) Le ɣeyiɣi aɖe megbe la, meva zu Yehowa Ðasefo.
ENGLISH: (2 Timothy 3:16) In time, I became one of Jehovah’s Witnesses.

ENGLISH: Why do you enjoy being one of Jehovah’s Witnesses?

ENGLISH: Our faith is not blind faith that ignores the facts of science

EWE: Xɔse si le mía si menye esi ŋea aɖaba ƒua nu siwo dzi dzɔdzɔmeŋutinunyalawo ɖo kpee la dzi o.
ENGLISH: Our faith is not blind faith that ignores the facts of science.

ENGLISH: Also, the principles that guide us are firmly based on the Bible.

ENGLISH: As one of Jehovah’s Witnesses, I enjoy sharing the Bible’s comforting message with others and helping them to find answers to their questions.

ENGLISH: A Mathematician Explains His Faith

ENGLISH: For years he was one of the most published authorities on statistics, a field in which he is still involved.
